Thought- fully picking himself up he remarked: "I wonder what noise that was I just heard?" THE fact that we can't take our money with us when we die is a great consolation to the legal profession. JORKINS : "What arc you thinking so hard about ? " Perkins: "I am trying to decide which a man derives the most real enjoyment from—lazi- ness or conceit."

FATTIER (who has helped his son in school work): " What did the teacher remark when you showed him the translation ?" Johnny: "He said I was getting mote stupid every (lay." " THERE is something im this little fellow I like,' eaid an at reciative visitor to a young hopeful he was trotting on his knees. "Now," said the boy, "how did you know I had swallowed a shilling?" "DID you ever see a horse race that you could say was absolutely honestly run ?" "I think I did, wunst," said Bill. "The feller that won it had stolen the boss, and he kept ahead of us." LAERVJg : "I hear yer got caught tryin' ter steal a foller's chainless bicycle, Las' -night." Sorry Sawyer : "Yes. 1 didn't know there was a chainless dorg in the yard." THICRE are two kinds of laz:ness—active and passive. The passively lazy man does nothing, or as near it as circumstances will permit; the actively lazy man shirks the work he ought to do, but spends his time doing something else. Too WEIGHTY COMPLIATENTS.—" What was this row about?" said the policeman. "It all came about," the father-in-law explained, "by some of those cheeky boys throwing shoes at the bride." "Well," said the policeman, "that's customary." " Yes ; but not horseshoes." _

IN THE WEATHER BUREAU.—The youthful pro- phet was plainly mortified. He had just been appointed, and his first prediction had not been verified. "The reason we didn't have that storm" —be explained, earnestly. "Hush ! " inter- rupted his aged superior. "In this business we never stop to apologise. Just guess again." Travelling Tank: "I was readin' a piece de udder day about a man hypnertisin' a feller an' makin' him commit a crime. It fairly made me blood run cold." Wallar : " Gittin' purty good all of a sudden, ain't ye?' Travelling Tank: "No; but if they kin do that an' make a feller commit a crime, they kin make him work. I tell ye, nobody's safe 1" TRIED AND NOT FOUND WANTING.—" Young Populare is the most self-possessed man lever saw. He neeer gets the least bit unnerved under any cir- cumstances." "Why, in what exigency did you ever see him tried, to have sucli confidence in him?" "I saw him exhibiting his first baby to half a dozen women at once, and answering every question rationally," A PRlZE.—Bricker Brack : " Now,this is the most valuable piece of porcelain in my collection—worth at least £50." Visitor: "Why, it's beer broken and repaired 1" Bricker Brack : "Yes, that's just what makes it so valuable. It was broken into a hundred fragments, and it cost me £5O to have it put together THE FORCE OF HABIT. A widower is being married for the fourth time. During the ceremony one of the guests is surprised to hear violent sobs proceeding from a woman in a corner of the church. "Who is that woman who is crying so bitterly?" he asks of the bystanders. "Oh, it's only Martha our cook," answers one of the bridegroom's children; "she always blubbers when papa gets married." HE KNEw..—" Do you know what conservatories are for, Willie ? " asked his uncle. "You bet I do," replied the boy, promptly; and then, turning to his sister, he asked: "Shall I tell them, Mammie ? " That being the first intimation she had had that he had been in or near the con- servatory the evening before, naturally she blushed. _

"The rummiest marster I ever ad," said a game- keeper, "wur t'ould Parson Sharp. He wur as blind as a bat, be wur." "And did he go shooting ? " asked one of the interested audience. " Shootin'? Yss—he shot reglar. But he couldn't -see, he couldn't. When anythin' rose, I used to cry -.Birds, sir I' and then I'd run behind parson, and the dogs 'ud run behind me, and we'd all go dancin' round behind t'ould gentleman, while he blazed away with both bads." SHE was one of the new mistresses, anxious to make a real home for her servant, and she allowed Mary's young man to call every Wednesday evening and stay to supper. "Your young man seems a very nice, quiet young fellow, Mary; I never hear a sound when he is in the kitchen." "Yes, m'm," answered Mary, with a simper, "you see, m'm, he's very bashful as yet, and when he comes he does nothing but eat." "Tins animal, ladies and gents," said the show- man, "is the chimpanzee. The remarkable thing about the chimpanzee, ladies and gents, is that it vomes nearest to being a human person of any epeeshy of the monkey tribe. This here is the chimpanzee, ladies and gents," he continued, "the one inside the cage. Piease stand a little further back, sir! You'll get mixed." And he glared at a masher who was poking the animal with his cane.

NOT BUILT VI T WAY. —At a railway station in Kent, the door of the carriage was opened to admit a tall man with a slender girth, who tried to wedge himself in between two burly farmers; but, finding it hard, he said: "Excuse me, sir, but you must sit up a bit. Each seat is made for five persons, and accord- ing to Act of Parliament, you are only entitled to eighteen inches of room." "My good air, said the farmer, "although you have been fortunate enough to be constructed according to Act of Parliament, you can hardly blame me if I am not built that way." AND Now HE NEEDN'T Go.—" Now, Georgie, you mustn't put it off any longer Go to papa this afternoon and tell him what you want." "Yes, I know I must. Let me see. Is your papa's desk in the middle of the room ?" "No ; it's against the wall in the corner furthest from the door." "1 see. The door is opposite the desk. There is no way that he could run around and get behind a fellow, is there?" "Why, George, how you talk 1" "Well, I know what Pm talking about. I don't want to slide into any office and then find that the old man is nearer the door than I am. That very thing happened to me the last time, and " "George 1" GOOD SWURITY. A small farmer went into a bank in Limerick, when the follow- ing conversation took place between him and the manager: "Good inornin', yer hcriner ; I called about a little business, and though there's other banks in the town I thought I'd give yer honner the compliment." "Well, Tom, I'm glad to see you ; and what's the business?" "I hear the interest in Widow Brady's farm is to be sould soon, yer honner, and I want to rise 'five hundbred poun' to buy it." "Nonsense, Tom, how could you ever pay the money back, if I lent it to you?" "On, there's nothin' aster in life. Shure me young Jim ud get it in a brimn when he marries." "And may I ask, Tom, what age is the young fellow?" "He's just three years (mid, yer honner I" "Miss Goldie," he began, with a brave attempt at calmness, "if I had had anything to do with arranging the decorations, I think I should have hung the mistletough boa"— Smiling at this slip of the tongue, and trying not to appear flustered, he quiokly continued "1 think I should have hung the mistle boe tough " Pausing for a moment to collect his thoughs, he smiled faintly and repeated, "should have hung the mistlebough toe" Embarrased, but riot discouraged, the young man started again : "Have hung hung the bistle- tough mough"--.-- Here, it was plainly apparent, he was uncertain whether it behoved him to make another trial or not. He would probably have dropped the subject entirely if it had not been for the yound lady's look of encouragement, which he took as evidence that something further in the same line was expected. During the brief respite which this thought gave him, the absurdity of it all struck him forcibly, and resuming his remarks with more confidence, he said; "I merely intended to observe that it would have been much nieer to have hung the tistlemae bough—er—l mean the " " George, dear, said the young lady kindly, "the step-ladder has been returned to the cellar. Don't you think it would be easier to mote the sofa over underneath the mistletoe f"
My DEAR NELLIE,

On every hand it must be frankly acknowledged that pretty hats abound this summer. One of the most attractive is a high crowned shape of Panama straw, the broad brim of which is covered with black lace and bound with black velvet. Another band of velvet goes round the crown, and two big choux bows of cream chiffon, a velvet rosette and a little branch of deep red cherries complete the trimming. A pretty variation of this hat has for trimming a garland of shaded pink and cream roses and bows of cream tulle veiled with black lace. Rush hats are worn at all times for all occasions, the most useful being very simply trimmed with fans of glace silk; but a smarter kind is a round shape deeply bound with black or coloured velvet, and trimmed with French quills on each side of a big front rosette of either velvet, chiffon, or tulle. A most fascinating. variety of hat has a high Tuscan crown, and a brim of frilled cream muslin with one large, or two small, rosettes of coloured tulle nestled among the kilt- ings on the left side. For toques, finely-tucked glace silk is largely used, as is tucked chiffon.

In a bodice of a new and pretty shape the upper portion simulates a zouave, and again, on the shoulders, a little cape-collar. The lower part has straight lines of stitching, and pointed fronts, with buttons at either side, not meant as fasten- ings, but merely as trimming. The chemisette is embroidered muslin, lined with silk. A long black silk tie is so arranged as to define this chemisette at the sides, the ends falling almost to the waist, round which a shaped black silk belt is fastened. A soft woollen material that was once called llama, is now known as foule. The skirt in a dress of this colour has stitched seams, which open below the knees to show spotted woollen fabric arranged in pleats. This spotted material forms the vest, across which the fronts are caught with three little straps made of the foul& The buckles are enamel. Plain white cloth forms the facing of the collar, with two rows of stitching in the khaki colour. Three tucks at the top relieve the rather dragged look of the sleeve, and at the wrist are the new under-sleeves in silk muslin, the over-sleeves widening above them.

Unbleached linen gowns with Eton coats, and vests of blue or red linen, are smart and pretty, but an Eton coat rarely stands washing and iron- ing without getting hopelessly out of shape. The white pique gowns with cuffs and collars of coloured linen are much more serviceable, as they are generally made with full, loose bodices, to which the facings are only tacked. Other favourite materials for holiday gowns are alpaca and cream or white serge. This year the first is particularly popular in blue and light fawn, the latter shade being especially useful when long and dusty jour- neys by rail are undertaken. The white serges are usually made in the bolero or Eton style with mul- titudinous rows of stitchings or strappings, and smart blouse-vests. The sailor-hat seems at the moment to be a little out of favour; at least, it has more serious rivals than it has had for many a long day. Boat-shaped hats of Panama and various other kinds of straw, in all shades from white to tan, ace extremely fashionable, and are trimmed in most instances with a scarf and bow of either soft brocade or glace silk.

Althoup thN coat and skirt costume, whether in serge or cloth, is the most comfortable for travelling wear, another style of make is much in favour this holiday season. This has a stitched skirt of the usuat sort, but instead of a coat there is a pouched bodice, fastening with very small buttons down the left side of the front, after the manner of the Russian blouse, and finished at the top with a deep, carefully-fitted, falling collar of the material, covered with rows of stitching. The sleeves are of the modernised Garibaldi shape, with tight-stitched wrist-bands, and the deep corslet belt is of stitched glace silk. This travell- ino, dress should be provided with a cape made of the same material, ornamented with rows of stitching and lined with glace. Bathing dresses I am told, grow smarter with every year. We have borrowed from France many good ideas about them. The old-fashioned "gown" that was made tight round the neck, and nearly strangled its wearer when it got wet, is still to be occasionally seen. It is not always the fittest things that enjoy the longest survivaL But the up-to-date gown, made in two parts, the tunic of which frees the neck, while the sleeves cover only the top of the arms, is now universally chosen. One of the smartest has revers of white striped and sky blue striped flannel, the material of the gar- ment itself being navy serge. The interval between the revers is filled in with the flannel, an anchor embroidered upon it in navy blue. Another is trimmed so as to siniulate a deep sailor collar. The pretence is preferable to the reality, which has a way of blowing up round the head which is far from comfortable. The skirt of the tunic is usually king enough to reach almost to the edge of the short knicker-bockers, which finish at the knees. Your loving JENITne.

Yet another crushing blow has fallen upon our beloved Queen in the loss of her second son, the Duke of Saxe- Coburg-Gotha. For some time past his Royal Highness had been a great ufferer, going from one place to Another in search of health, which was denied him—but no one imagined the end to be 9 near. The Duchess I has never fully recovered from the wbock of her son's death, and much sympathy is felt for her in this further sad bereavement. Or the four daughters el the late Duke of Sine Coburg only one is unmarred, the Princess Beatrice, who is eixteen years of age. The others are the Crown Princess of Roumania, the Grand Duchess of Hesse, and the Princessof Hoheelohe-Laugenburg, whose husband the Hereditary Prince is euardian to the young Duke of Albany—heir presumptive—during his miaority. All three were married almost from the schoolroom, and there have been rumours of late that Princess Beatrice is to follow her sistere example when she reaches her seventeenth birthday, in April next. Toe greatest sympathy is also felt for the widowed Queen Marguerite, whose married life with the late King of Italy was one of singular happiness and devotion. The King was only fifty-six years old, so that he might reasonably have looked forward to a long period of use- , fulness among his people. The Queen who was also the cousin of her husband, is the only daughter of the late Prince Ferdinand of Savoy, and she married King Humbert is 1868. Their only son, the Prince of Naples, who now succeeds to the Italian throne' was born in the following year, and is therefore just on 31 years of age. He was married in 1898 to the Princess Helena a daughter of Nicholas, Prince f Montenegro. The dastardly crime which has thus been the means of calling him to the throne, once more emphasises the unenviable notoriety achieved by Italian Anarchies. It was an Italian who killed President Carnot in 1894. It was also an Italian who stabbed the Empress of Austria in 1898, and though Sipido, who shot at the Prince of Wales last April belongs to a Belgian family, it is said that be comes from Italian sterk. Like all these , criminals, the murderer of King Humbert is a young man, and it is not unlikely that he was influenced in his act by the disgraceful miscarriage of justice in Belgium which has allowed Sipido to regain his liberty. Queen Marguerite's daughter-in-law,the present Queen of Italy is a very beautiful and amiable woman. Both she and the king have tke same tastes, the same pur- suits, and unless separated by duty are constantly in each other's society. The Queen's taste in dress is fault- less, she ranking, and deservedly, among the best dressed Royalties of Europe Only seldom has her Majesty been persuaded to don the Montenegrin national costume since her marriage. This is one of barbaric magnificence, being heavily embroidered with gold and uncut gems of great size. Golden fringes and st quins hang from the sleeves, waistband, and ends of the sash, and the Greek jacket and little cap are one mass of gold. Lady Randolph Churchill's wedding presented many reminiscences of the war. Both the bride and bride- groom know comething about it, as Mr. Cornwallis West had been invalided home from his regiment at the front, while Lady Randolph Churchill has been out in charge of the nursing arrangements on board the Maine. Many distinguished people home from the war were also present, including Lady Sarah Wilson who was in Mafeking during the long seige, the Duke of Marl- borough, Mr. Winston Churchill, and many others. The assisting clergyman was a cousin of Major-General Baden-Powell, and the bride was given away by her nephew the Duke of Marlborough. In tbie respect the Duke his had a singular experience for not only has he had to give away his aunt the wick w of his father's only brother, but he also had the giving away •of his step- mother. when the second wife of his father married Lord William Beresford. The wedding was productive of a large number of presents, many of Lady Randolph's friends clubbing together to present her with a handsome piece of jewellery. This suggests whether some organisation of wedding presents wauld not be generally practicable so that the multiplication of salt cellars, butter dishes' claret jugs, etc., might be avoided. The selection of presents is usually a difficult matter to settle, and every- one knows how apt people are to make the same choice, thus leading to a more or lees useless duplication of the same article. It is not eaey to see how anything like a formal arrangement could be made. At the same time it is °ltem possible to obtain a hint from friends or rela- tives, and it is always worth while to take some trouble to ensure that one's present will.be really useful. Numbers of women have been wearing artificial, scented filwers, tucked in the bodice lately,and so faith- fully are these blossoms copied from nature, that it is almcst impossible to distinguish the imitation from the real. No objection to the custom of wearing artificial flowers in our headgear has ever been raised, and it is difficult to understand why it bas so long been deemed undesirable to place them in one's bodice. It is almost impossible to detect the scented specimens, and more- over they retain their freshness, an item indeed worthy of our consideration. Collars, where summer outdoor gowns are concerned are conspicuous by their absence. A soft little frill finishes off the bodices at the neck, above which usually appears a narrow velvet band, fastened with some jewelled clasp. In a few instances tulle or chiffoneirawn through jewelled slides has taken the place of the velvet hand, but this idea is by no means as successful. In the first place it is net a cool arrangement, and secondly it gives one, unless very carefully carried out, a somewhat untidy appearance. One is frequently reminded in some initarces of the nursery cat,after little fingers have been busy in its adornment. Mrs. Garnett Anderson, M.D., did well to emphasize at a recent meeting of the College for Working Women, the ennrmons importance of obtaining as much fresh air as possible. Of course every right minded person feels intense sympathy for the poor folks who are overcrowded in slums, but it involves no lack of sympathy to remark that the unhealthiness of overcrowding could be miti- gated very considerably by the free admission of air. It is easy to understand that in the winter poor people with insufficient clothes wish to get all the warmth they can bv closing the windows, but in weather such as we have had lately there is every reason for opening win- dows and doors widely. I Nor do Dr. Anderson's observations apply only to the _ _

pror, for there are thousands of people- siith Moderate siz,doind large houses who sleep throughout the hottest nights with their windows cloßed. If they would try for a month in the summer the effect of opening their bedroom widows as widely as popsible, they would find that tbeir sleep would be much more refeeshinv, and would be scarcely likely to resume their former practice of shutting out one of their best friends.

div.head: WARRINGTON DRUIDISM.
div.p: WARRINGTON DRUIDISM.
Presentation of Chains of Office.

An interesting ceremony in connection with the War- rington District of the Order of Druids took place at the Druids' Hall, Sankey-st,ret on Monday evening. Owing to the generosity of Deputy District Grand 111 aster Edward Allen,vrho is a member of the Fearnhead Lodge, the D'strict Officers were each presented with handsome chains of office, the Grand Treasurer of the Order, Mr Godfrey Ffigham, of Brookkeels, near Manchester, per- forming the ceremony of investing them with the realia The recipients of the chains were the District Grand Master C Bebbington, Deputy Di,trict Grand Master Alien, District Treasurer S Dunbobbin and District Secretary D Houghton. The chains were artistically designed, the one presented to the Grand Master being of gold and the others of silver. A pendant bearing the emblem of the order was attached to each and the links were in the form of shields on which could he engraved , the mimes of the holders of the chain year by year. In investing the officers with the chains the Grand Treasurer characterized the occasion as being unique. He had frequently been iequested to make presentations to brethren in honour of rervices rendered by them but he had never had the pleasure of being called upon to inveet the officers of a di,trict with such beautiful regalia as the chains which were being presented that evenine. He recollected that many years ago people used to say that their ecei ties were made up of men who went shout the streets fikuetine banners and regalia which were very expensive, and had been purchased at the expense of the members. He was pleased to say that not one single farthing cf the funds of the district had been trespassed upon to obtain those chains- (Applause.) In investing the Grand Master with the gold chain lie ' bad not the slightest doubt he would feel hanpy to recall the fact that be was the first officer of the district to wear it. He felt assured that the abilities Mr Betbiegton had displayed during his career as a Druid would he continued until the conclusion of his peried of office, and that he would so conduct the business of the • district that the chain would be handed down unsullied to his successor. Nothing could be more conducive to the interests of the Order, or couTd reflect more credit upon him than the fact that be had endeavoured te deal fairly and honestly with the members with whom he was identified. (Applause). The Gre,d Trrawir, r then invested 0.1) G M. Allen, District Treasurer nunbobbin and Disrrict Secretary Houehron with ,11-• silver chainF, aderesaing suitable reml,les to each of the recipients. Past Dietrict Officer LANGLEY proposed a vote ef *thanks to the Grand Treasurer for performing the core- mory and expressed the gratitude of the members for his presence that evening. P ROUGBLEY seconded the proposition which was carried with acclammation

Mr RIONAM briPfiv aCknOwlrdged the compliment. The retnainrier of 'he evening was epent in a convivial manner, a capital progr mme being rendered incluclinv ''umorous songs by Megn.s. Fineh and Ernson and violin and pianoforte duets by the M'sies Prtoley. At the conclusion a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Bro Allen for his valuable gift to the dis- trict- on the motion of Bro HOUGHTvN seconded by the Senior Trustee.

div.head: TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
div.p: THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
BY JOSEPH HOCKING,
Author of "The Birthright," "Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," &c.
CHAPTER XV.
"MAN PROPOSES, BUT GOD DISPOSES."

"Well, what do you think of Rutland ? " asked Father Sheen of Father Ritzoom, as the two men sat together in the study of the former the day following the visit to the Priory. "I think that which confirms my first impres- sions concerning him," replied the Jesuit. "I think it is a great pity that such as he should be a heretic, and I am sure we shall be rendering the cause of our Church a great service by leading him to accept the faith." "You think you will succeed, then ? " "I think the sun will rise to-morrow morning." replied Ritzoom, "and I think that two and two make four." "I am not so sure," replied Father Sheen, shaking his head. "That is." he added, seeing the Jesuit laugh, "I am not so sure that Rutland will be converted." "Did I not know that you were of pure Celtic origin I should believe you had some taint of Anglo-Saxon blood in you," remarked Ritzoom. "An Englishman is generally certain when he should be doubtful, and doubtful when he should be certain. He can swear to a material demonstra- tion, but never to a moral certainty. He can understand that a piece of steel can be attracted by a magnet, because he can appreciate physical forces, but he cannot be just as certain that a man of a certain disposition will yield to certain influences. To me one is no less certain than the other." "But human nature is a very complex business." "So is a piece of machinery to a man who doesn't understand it. Everything is resolvable into some primary motive or principle; once under- stand that and all becomes plain. Besides, I believe in Providence."

"What do you mean ? " "Oh, simply that Providence sent that Arthur Stanley to the Priory last night. Providence caused Alizon to greet him heartily. It brings matters to a speedy climax." "In what way ? " 'Did you not see Rutland's face last night ? "

"I saw nothing particular." "Sheen, you must be an Englishman. You could not be so dense otherwise. The fellow is already in love with her. He may not realise it yet, but he will in a day or two." "How—how do you know?" "How do I know that a man will laugh when you tickle him? By the way, did he say any- thing to you about Stanley? Did he ask you any questions? " "I really have forgotten: but I know I told him that he was an aspirant for .Alizon's hand." "Ah, did you? Well ? " "I thought he took it quietly; stay, though, his voice was rather husky. But he changed the subject immediately after I had told him." "Just so. He asked questions about me, didn't he ? " "My word, Ritzoom ! But to tell the truth, he did. How did you know ? " The Jesuit laughed quietly. "I don't think he slept much last night," he said presently. "You believe then that--" "I believe you are the most simple-minded fellow in the world, Sheen. You are too good to live." "And you are the cleverest fellow I know. I wish you had met him in debate instead of my poor ignorant self. You would have pulverised him. Last night he said ditto to nearly everything you said." "Yes, and saw the fallacy of it all. Had I uttered those sentiments in a public meeting he would have torn them to pieces. No, no, things are better as thug stand." "Well, but what is the next move in the game you are playing for this man's soul ? " "I shall make no move."
"And he?" "Well, I am not sure; but I don't think he will make any move." "Then what are we to do ? "

"Wait." Meanwhile, Duncan Rutland sat alone in his lodgings. As Father Ritzoom had said, he had not slept a wink during the night, and now, as he crouched before the fire, his head resting on his hands, he looked worn out and ill. His face was very pale, while around his eyes dark rings had gathered. The revelation of his love had come upon him suddenly, and it had almost stunned him. He had been playing with dangerous weapons, and had not known it. Never dreaming of the plot of which he was the victim, he had gladly gone to the Priory, and at each visit he had yieldeA more and more to the spell of a young girl's eyes. He did not know of the subtle influence which was working in his nature. He had thought of Alizon Neville as a beautiful, cultured girl, one who welcomed him kindly and made his every visit pleasant. In spite of the fact that she regarded him as an enemy to truth, or perhaps it was because she so regarded him, he was much interested in her; but the thought of loving her had never entered his mind. Her social position, her wealth, her antagonism to his faith, made it out of the question. He had felt no pang of jealousy when Arthur Stanley catne into the room—it was too absurd; nor, perhaps, would his secret have been revealed to him had not father Sheen told him of Stanley's hopes. Then the truth came to him, and stunned him. He knew he loved her, knew that his life would be barren and utterly dreary without her. She had kindled a fire in his heart which could never be extinguished, the whole wealth of his life had gone out to her, and without her the future seemed but a dreary mockery. "Everything is against it," he cried, as at length he started from his chair and began to pace the room. "Everything, everything! I belong to a class which does not mate with that to which she belongs. She is an aristocrat, lam a commoner. She is rich. lam poor—and yet I love her! Even although it were possible for her to love me, she could never be the wife of a Non- conformist minister. She is the only daughter of Lady Neville, an ardent Catholic. No, no, I must fl&*lit it—kill it!" He seized his hat and went 'Out. He could not breathe in his little study, the air was hot and stifling. A few minutes later he was out on the moors, where the wind swept freely, and the air smelt sweet and pure. He walked for hours, but he did not grow tired, nor did his eyes cease to burn with an unnatural light. Again and again did he declare that he would cast his love from him as a painful mockery, and as often did he find himself hugging it to his breast as the joy of life. It was the old ,tnry. A man fighting against the dictates of I:; heart, and being defeated. The very habits of his life made his love more hopeless. He had not been accustomed to the society of women; he had had no love affairs. Had he, his present passion would not have been so strong, so overwhelming. From nineteen to twenty-six he had lived in his class-rooms and among his books. He had come to Lynford ignorant of the master passion of life, and no member of his congregation had stirred his heart. Now—the flood-gates of his heart had been opened wide and he was helpless. He felt thankful for those wild, wide moors, snd when he had got miles away from the town, so far that no signs of life were visible, he stood and looked around him. The sight was almost awe- inspiring; everywhere as far as the eye could reach the bare moorland stretched around him, rising and falling like great billows. Sometimes it seemed to him like a mighty sea, while he was alone, "all, all alone." Above, the grey sky spread itself, chill, gloomy, oppressive. Scarcely a streak of blue was to be seen. No sound was to be heard save the wailing of the wind, and an occasional cry of the moor birds. "Of course she never dreams of such a thing," he cried presently. "It is absurd to think of it; it is worse than absurd, it is madness. Oh, I must kill itt I must kill itl " He knelt down on the soft, springy turf and cried aloud. "0 God, hear me!" he cried. "0 God, help me!" But the wailing wind and the shriek of the moor birds were the only answer that he heard to his prayer. And yet his wild cry helped him. It made him realise the fact that he was not alone. The Spirit of God was on those wild moors, and that Spirit cared for him.

div.head: AUGUST
div.p: AUGUST

flour atter flour !ie stayed out there alone. .tsy• and-bye the rain fell, and the winds blew louder, but he did not heed. He partook of no food, but be felt neither faint nor hungry. He tried to formulate his plans, tried to think .)1 means whereby his mad passion could be destroyed. He remembered the words of old Matthy Bray. Yes, he would find a wife! That would be it. He would drive the thought. of Alizon Neville from his mind. This was his manifest duty. When he married he must have a wife who would help him in his church, and who would be received by the members of his congregation. Yes, the eldest Miss Ashton would make a suitable minister's wife. She was nearly his own age, she had received a conventional , education; she was pious, and had been connected with Tudor Chapel all her life. She was wealthy, too. She would receive ten thousand pounds for her wedding dowy, and her position in the town was assured. Everyone would declare that his choice was wise. He did not think she would refuse him; apparently she delighted in his company, and would not refuse to he mistress of his home. At least, he hoped not. As for the thought of marrying Alizon Neville, it was utter madness. Fancy her marrying a Protestant minister—it would outrage the religious life of the town. Yes, that must be his plan. He would drive her from his mind, and in order to do --.7.1; he would call at Mr. Ashton's that very night.

lie reached his lodgings about eight o'clock in the evening, and then, realising that his clothes were wet, he changed them, and afterwards went to Mr. Ashton's house. As he expected, he was met with a hearty welcome. The Lancashire people are among the most hospitable in the world; besides, Duncan was their minister, and was beloved by every member of the family. He did his best to enter into the pleasures of the evening. He laughed loudly, he told stories, he sought the company of the eldest Miss Ashton, and did his best to make himself agreeable. The eldest Miss Ashton was evidently pleased at Duncan's behaviour; she sung the two songs she knew best, and reached a very high note at the conclusion of "Killarney ".—a note which had never failed to draw a cheer at the concerts held at Tudor schoolroom. Miss Ashton was renowned for this song. It was regarded as her song, and she had sung it scores of times with about as much feeling as an organ- grinder puts into the music which he grinds to order. Duncan cheered the song greatly. He had heard her sing it several times before, just as the previous minister had heard it, but his applause was none the less hearty. Then she sung her other song, "Ora Pro Nobis," which she rendered in just the same way as she had rendered the other. He had heard it on every barrel organ in the town, it had been sung at almost every concert he had attended. Under other circumstances he would have felt like laughing. Miss Ashton was stout and florid. Her face was placid, there was no passion in her nature. She ate well, she slept well, and was as little able to sing such a song as she was able to sing that wondrous solo, "Hear My Prayer," which Alizon Neville had sung with so much feeling the night before. The picture of the young girl came back to him, and he could not help comparing her with this buxom young woman who went on woodenly repeating both music and words. No, he could not carry out his plans. It would be sacrilege to try and pretend to love her. How could this commonplace girl, good and true as she undoubtedly was, drive from his heart that which had so completely mastered him ? He left Mr. Ashton's ho • se early, and for several days after he was not seen except at the meetings he was obliged to attend. Every day, wet or fine, he went out on the moors, as though they fascinated him. He did not go near the Priory; sometimes he climbed the hills and looked down at the old house which nestled among the trees; but he went no nearer, he dared not. He called to mind what Father Sheen had said about "A Retreat," and wondered what it meant. He fancied Alizon kneeling in the little chapel and praying amidst a great silence. He neNer intended, or expected to tell Alizon Neville of the love which she had inspired in his heart, nor, indeed, did he take any steps in order to see her. Indeed, nearly a month passed away, and he kept away, from the old house, then when the spring had fairly come he went across the moors in the very direction he had gone when he had first spoken to her. He was passing through the farm- yard where he had heard her talking with the farmer's wife, when he saw her coming towards him from the farm-house. • The blood surged into his pale cheeks, and his heart seemed as though it would burst. Still he mastered himself, and when Alizon Neville held out her hand to him he seemed fairly cool and collected. "You have forsaken us, Mr. Rutland," said the girl, kindly. "gave you been especially busy? " "No," replied Rutland, "no, I have done practically no work for a month." "Then why have you not been to see us? Have you been ill? " "Yes—no—that is, I don't know." She looked at him keenly. bewildered her, "Has anything teen troubling you?" she asked, kindly. "Yes," he replied. "I am so sorry; but your trouble has passed, I hope ? " "No, it has not passed." He spoke roughly, almost rudely. • "I am so sorry," she said again, will soon be gone." • "No, 'it will never be gone." "Never be gone ? " "No, never." He had not meant to speak in this way, but the girl's presence seemed to drag the words from him. "Are you ill? Excuse me, I will gladly help you if I can." He walked on by her side sometime without speaking, while the girl wondered what ailed him. "I must tell you," he said at length. "I did not mean to, and doubtless you will be angry with me, aye, scorn me, but I cannot help it. Heaven knows I have fought against it, fought with all my strength —but it is no use." She had no idea of what was in his mind. That he should dream of loving her had never appeared to her even as a dim possibility. She fancied that he might be worried about his church work. Of course it was that, or (and her heart beat with joy at the thought of it), was the truth revealing itself to him? Yes, that was it. He had become dissatisfied with Protestantism, the truths of her religion had mastered him, even while he was a Protestant minister. She had prayed for this so earnestly, prayed that he might be led to stand up in the Industrial Hall and confess his error. It had seemed too good to be true, but God was good, and had answered her prayers sooner than she had dared to hope. "Yes, tell me, Mr. Rutland," she said, kindly, me everything. Perhaps I can help you." You will be angry with me." "Oh no, I will not; tell me. Perhaps I know more of what is in your heart than you think," and she looked up into his face with a kindly smile. "Very well," said Duncan, his heart throbbing mightily at her words, "I will tell you."
His manner
CHAPTER XVI.
"but perbapp it
RUTLAND'S CONFESSION.

"Everything can be told in three words," said the young man, after hesitating a few seconds. "I love you." "What!" There was consternation, disappointment, anger, expressed in the word. "Just that, Miss Neville. Oh, I knew you would be angry! " he continued, as he looked into her face. "I know lam mad; I know that what I say must seem to you preposterous. But I cannot help it. For a month I have been fighting against it. I have told myself that I am a fool, a madman. But I cannot destroy the feeling. I know that you resent my making this confession. 1 am nothing to you but an heretic, to whom in the goodness of your heart, you have been kind, but I cannot help it. I did not mean to tell you, but in this, too, I have been weaker than a child. Oh, forgive me, Miss Alizon! " The girl answered never a word. The blood had ntled to her face, and her lips were tremulous. :one had never thought of the ycung man in this way, nevertheless she could not listen to his words without being moved. She instinctively felt that they were honest. He meant what he had said, and there was something overmastering in his presence. She admired him, cared for him far more than for Arthur Stanley, who was anxious for her to be his wife. He was more of a man in every way. Personally, he was more than the equal of the young squire, while intellulaially the poles were between them. Had they belonged to the same-, but there, as he had said, his con- fession was absurd, and yet it was not unpleasant toza hear. He might be a commoner, but he was a gentleman, and no girl is insensible to an honest sane love.

"You are angry," said Duncan. "No," said the girl, "that is--" "I am so glad," he cried, "so glad." He looked into her eyes. lie saw that they were humid, and that her lips trembled. A great hope came into his heart. rerhaps—perhans she might care for him. His love made him bold.. "Thari.l you," he interrupted. "It is kind of you to hear me, at least, with patience. I am afraid my love is hopeless." "It is," said the girl, scarcely realising what she said. "At the,same time—that is--" "What ? " cried Duncan. "Oh, believe me, this is no passing fancy! I never loved a woman before. I never pretended to. I have never been thrown among young girls at all. During the years I was a student I lived for study; but—but you have changed everything--everything. Oh, I know I am foolish, but I cannot help it. I love you with my whole heart, my whole life. I know lam asking you what seems impossible; but you know that old Latin saying: Oinnia vincit anwr.' Is there any possibility that it can be true? Can my love overcome all things? Can I, by years of devotion, win your love for me?" Alizon did not speak. The young man's words had moved her more than she thought possible. After all, his words were—but no-- "It is impossible—impossible, Mr. Rutland; think no more of it. You bring pain on both us by persisting. Had I dreamt that you WCO4 ever have cared for me in this way, I would %it,- have--" _

But she did not finish the sentence. She had meant to say that she would not have invited him to the Priory if she had thought that he would have fallen in love with her; but she was not sure about it, for she was very anxious for his con- version. And while she would not have participated in the plot of Ritzoom had it been revealed to her in its entirety, she was still prepared to sacrifice much in order to save his soul, and win a victory for the Church.

"Are you sure it is impossible ? " said Duncan, pleadingly. "Think again. No one could love you more truly, devotedly, than I shall love you throughout my life. I would give my life to make you happy. Don't discard me hastily. Think— may you not at some time learn to care for me ? " He was excited beyond measure, and did not see the thousand difficulties which stood in the way of the love he asked for.
Alizon hesitated a second. She longed too earnestly for his conversion to wound him; besides, during the last few weeks she felt more kindly towards him.

"It is no use my thinking, Mr. Rutland," she said at length, "even if I—l loved you I should have to—to destroy it. The very thought of such 8 thing would be madness." "Why?" asked the young man. Now that the ice was broken, he felt bolder. Difficulties did not seem so formidable, and his. love did not seem foolish.
"Surely you can see yourself ? " she said. "No, I cannot. That is—if you loved me nothing would be impossible. I could brave any- thing, overcome everything." "But, but--"

"You mean the social gulf that lies between us. I am a Nonconformist minister, while you possess an old name. You are, I suppose, rich, and I am poor. No, I had not thought of that. Love would overcome all that. Do yen mean that?" "No," said the girl, "I do not mean that. Sucu a thing would not have weight with me. I am enough of a Radical to know that neither poverty nor riches can make a gentleman, while I have known men bearing old names who—but I did not mean that. There is something of more importance than that. Surely you can think ? " "No, no—not if you could love me," said Duncan. "You are not one who is carried away with mere surface things. If von loved me—yes, you would brave the anger of all you hold dear." "But I could not brave my conscience." "Your conscience!" "Yee, my conscience. You forget that. Even if 1 loved you, I should feel it my duty to crush it, because it would be a sin." "A sin!" "Yes. How could it be otherwise? You are an enemy to my faith. Even in Lynford you have made perverts; -while in many hearts you have sown the seeds of doubt." "I see," said Duncan, sadly. "You would feel it your duty to destroy your love, because from your standpoint I am a heretic?" She did not reply, but walked by his side along the pathway through the fields. Strange to say, he had given no serious attention to this. If it had entered his mind he had dispelled it quickly. To him religious belief was a sacred thing, and while) he hated anything which savoured. of Sacer- dotalism, he had never regarded it in this light. "But—but—Protestants and Catholics have loved each other, and have—have married," he stammered presently. "I know it," she said, blushing; "neitlor does the Church absolutely forbid such unions. But to me it would be impossible. From my standpoint you are an unbeliever. Believe me, I do not mean— that is you see how utterly foolish it is for you !to—', "But," and Duncan interrupted her suddenly, and he hardly knew why he uttered the words which sprang to his lips, suppose this barrier did not exist, suppopf. I were a Catholic. suppose I could accept your faith in its entirety, what then? Could you ever learn to love tee then ? Tell me," persisted the young man, eagerly, "tell me! This is more to me than you can think." "Do you doubt your heresy ? " cried the girl. "Do you feel that you could give it up for me?" "I could give up anything, everything, for youz except the truth, and my own self-respect," he said. "But tell me, supposing I held your faith—what then?" "I do not know," said the girl, "I cannot tell. Pardon me, but I wish to be perfectly honest with you. I do not love you now. I never dreamt of such a thing. But I believe you to be sincere, and—and if you loved the faith I hold—l—l—that is I do not know." "Heaven bless you for saying eventhat," he cried, fervently. "But I can say nothing," replied the girl; "it would be wrong. Oh, please do not mistake me. I am afraid I am ignorant, foolish. But I believe you mean what you say, and no woman can think lightly of such words as those you have spoken!" She spoke excitedly, almost incoherently, and her words conveyed more to the young man than she really meant. "Heaven knows," he cried, "that you hold my happiness in the hollow of your hands. Humanly speaking, T live only for you. I never loved a woman before, and I shall never love another. I suppose other men have said all this, and then have broken their words; but they have never felt what I feel." "But I can promise nothing," said Alizon; "and—and—if you like, I will say nothing to anyone—that is about what you have said." The young man did not reply; his eyes rested on the Priory, which was embowered among the trr away in the distance. The sight seemed to cause all sorts of strange thoughts to come into his mind. "Do you think," said the girl, eagerly, "that you ever could change—that is, your opinions?" "No, I don't think so," said Duncan, quietly. No ? " "I think not. I think not. I would do any- thing in my power, even for the vague possibility of winning your love; but I do not think, even if you promised to marry me, that 1 could do that." She looked at him almost angrily. She had hoped from what he had said that there might be some hope. She had not given him a vestige of hope and yet her pride was touched. "Then you will do nothing?" she asked. "Oh, yes. I shall go over every inch of the ground. I shall study all that your best writers and teachers have to say, I shall leave no stone unturned in order to find the truth. Yes, I will confess it. I shall do this because you have not crushed all hope in my heart. I do not see even the vaguest possibility of my becoming a Catholic, but I will learn all that there is to be said in its favour.' "Will you ? " cried the girl, eagerly. "Will you go and hear our preachers and attend our Retreats? If you will you will see, you will learn, 1 am sure you will." "To do what I have promised seems tampering with the truth," said Duncan, quietly, "but t wifl go over the ground again. "Then ytu will be converted," cried the girl; eagerly. "Oh, if you knew the joy of faith; the utter contentment that it brings. If you could realise what I have felt when I have partaken of the blessed Sacrament, if you could know the joy of being sure that the saints were pleading for you, you would not hesitate a second." Duncan smiled sadly. From the earnest girl's standpoint, bith was easy; from his, however, all was different. Still, her presence made it possible. If such as she were the product of Catholicism, the thing could not be evil. They walked on together while the birds sang blithely'. &on in that smoky part of Lancashire.

Nature had clothed herselt in ter beauttlul garments of green, and the air was laden with the perfume of new life. Away in the distance they could see grimy Lynford, but the wind blew awaY the black volumes of sulphur and smoke, and e* they could rejoice in the beauty of God's day. • "Will you not come into the Priory it few minutes ? " said Alizon presently. "Father Ritzoom is still there, and Father Sheen is coming down this evening." Duncan looked at her questioningly. Ile felt very sensitive about meeting Lady Neville after the confession he had made. "Do you know," she went on, "that I shoull, like to regard what you have said to me as unsaid "It can never be unsaid," replied Duncan, I am glad now that I have dared to tell you WV' is in my heart." "What I meant was that nothing more need be said about it. I think I mentioned this sore° time ago." "Yes," replied Duncan; "but you have forgotteo Lady Neville." ,11 "No, I have not," said Alizon, blushing. / tell my mother everything, but I do not think need say anything about what you have told ree' Let us both agree to—to forget. That is, no orle need know." During their walk to Alizon's old home, Duncell did not once refer to what had been said; indeed, he spoke but little until they came to Bogert Clough. "You saved me from a great deal of rough bafldA ling here, Miss Neville," he said, as they SW" near the spot where the men had attacked him. "Please do not refer to it," said the girl, am angry with myself every time I think of it. "Angry with yourself for keeping those men fro' making--" "No, for uttering words which led them to 'a° such a thing. But I was terrlbly angry with 3109' Mr. Rutland. When I think of what you hey° done I am still. But you know us better non' don't you? "When I think of that night, I remember onlf your heroism," replied Duncan. "Whatever may be, the future of my life, I shall always be glad theb you were sufficiently interested in my welfare t° take a weary journey to save me from harm." , "Oh, but that was nothing. I could not beiP it," replied the girl. When they reached the Priory, Lady Nevii_Al° greeted the young minister kindly. She seer pleased to see him, and asked him to star tmn " evening. At first Duncan refused; but when heti; Alizon and Father Ritzoom seemed anxious for hi_t Lo stay, he consented. Perhaps Ritzoom had en more to do with his decision than Alizon, for tuw Jesuit possessed a strange influence. The re', always seemed to know more than he profesee"' while his very silence was suggestive of knowledg.% A little later a conversation took place whi; influenced Duncan more than at that thaie °- realised.
(To be continaed.)

Mr. Wedderburn : Very well, I will take it so. Con- tinuing counsel said that the first question that was taised in the petition of the London and North-Western -Railway Company was one which he did not think the c3tnmittee would find would really stand very much, namely, the necessity for a tramway. At any rate,for Present purposes, he would assume that was not a matter of preamble objection, but really a matter of Cause objection. Assuming that the tramway was there, the amount of traffic at present existing was Vready large,and at present that traffic crossed the rail- 'way on the level. Of course, that meant, that there `leas a considerable expense to the London and North- Western Railway Company in keeping up the level crossing; and in the working of the level crossing and they suggested in their petition that it would be a dangerous thing to have an elec. trical tram, ay on the level across their line but he should submit that there was nothing in it. If they could work it for the great traffic already going across, there was no more difficulty in working it for an electrical tramway goine across it than there would be 'Working it for those 160 'buses, and those pedestrians And vehicles to which he had referred. The question %mac as to whether it might not one day be necessary to 11'Y the road over the railway by a bridge. That .—Tht become necessary not only because of the con- r..uction of the tramway, but because of the increasing ,julffiC from the increase of the population and so on. 'uere was a special provision in the Act under which the tailway was constructed in 1851, which the company /tooted in their petition, namely, " That it shall be law- ttil for the Commissioners of Railways (substitute for them the 13,ard of Trade), if it shall appear to them necessary for the public safety at any time, either before or after the works hereby authorised to be made or any of them, shall have been completed, and opened for public traffie to require the company, within such time as the said dommissioners shall direct, and at the ex- pense of rhe company, to carry any or either of the bereinbefere mentioned roads, either under or over the railway by means of a bridge or atch instead of crossing the same on a level, or to execute such other Works ai under the Commissioners of the lease shall *Meer to the said Commissioners the best adapted to removing or diminishing the danger arising from any Ruch level crossing ; and if any of such works shall be Ireeptired by the said Commissioners before the railway Shall be completed then the railway shall not be opened tor the use of the public until such works shall have been executed and completed, as directed by the Commis- totters ;and if any of such works shall be required by the said Commissioners after the railway shall have been completed, then such works shall be executed by the Company within such time as shall be directed by the said Commissioners." The position of the Railway Company at the present moment was this, that if the traffic on this road became of such a nature as to make it undesirable that there should be a level crossing there, it would he open to the Board of Trade to say, either Yen must carry your line over the road, or you must carry it at your own expense over the line. It was thought that it might very well be that with the addi- tion of the tramway to the other traffic that was a con- tingency which was still more likely to arise, and therefore the question of this bridge came up before the other House, and of course the moment the question of the bridge came up the one material thing about it was this, neither of the railway companies could object to the fact of a bridge being there, any more than the Corporation could object to the fact of a bridge being there. But the usual question came up Who is to pay for it ? and whilst on the one side it was said the Cor- Poratien ought to pay the whale of it because it is your increasing traffic— Mr. Littler • No, no; all we said was that you ought not to have your tramway. Mr. Wedderburn : But when the queetion of cost Came up there were two arguments used. Mr. Littler : No.

Mr. Wedderburn : There were two arguments that could have been used, mne on the one side and one on the other. On the one side it could have been argued ,bat the necessity for this bridge arose because of the Increasing traffic and the public going along this road; the necessity for it was increased by the fact that the Corporation were putting down tramway/4 theretore it ratght be said that the Corporation should pay either all or the greater part of the cost. On the other hand, of course, the argument of the promoters was that the London and North Western Railway Company had the advantage of crossing the public road on a level and that at any time the Board of Trade if they thought it neckssary, might order the Company to build a bridge and pay the whole of the cost, of it. However, a middle course was taken by the House of Lords. What they said was this, that in the evtait f tae Board of Trade at any time hereafter, making an order that the road should be 9krried over the railway by means of a bridge then and in that case the Corporation should c instruct such works as might be necesary for carrying the road over the rail- Way according to plans previously submitted to the itondun and North-Western Ralway Co., and the com- pany should pay to the Corporation one half the cost of the maintenance of such works- Mr. Wedderburn again

Wedderburn : Then, sir, I think I have opened all I need say. We are ready to rest upon the clause as it stands, and I shall ask you when ou nave heard our evidence, to say that this tramway is necestary,aud that the clause is reasonably, and that the fair thing is that the Company and tne dorporation should bear the cost between them of the bridge. The Chairman: That is very important,and we have another rather conteatious Bill which is coming before us, and I would suggest to you whether you think it is necoasary ta call evidence- It seems to the Committee that it is really a matter for argument than' or eviuene,.. Mr. Weideiburn : lam quite ready to accept that in- timation. The only difficulty abent it is this,that if my learned friend, Mr. Littler is seriously going to cantend that thie tramway is not necessary, I suppose! must call evidence to show th,t it is. However, I hope that in mercy to the Committee, Mr. Littler will withdraw from that position. Mr. Littler: I connot withdraw from that position, but I will take it as shortly as I can. The Chairman : I may mention that I think this point, as far as my recollection gees, has been decided. and I should like to look at my decision, if possible, in the case of the Southport and Lytham Tramways, be- cause exactly the same question cropped up as to whether the road authorities should pay tor the widen- ingot the bridge, or whether the Canal Company should pay for the widening of tbe bridge, and if my impres- sion or recollection is right, this is an argument which affected us very much, namely,the road was an old road and was there first, and we decided that, at all events, the major portion, if not the whole of the cost, should be paid by the new corner. the Railway or Canal Com- pany I think it was. Mr. Ernest Moon : I was in that case, and the posi- tion thpre was that the bridge was going to be recon- structed. Now here, there is no reason for altering this road at all. The promoters of this scheme are prapos- log to run an electric tramway across the railway of the company, and but for their coming there it would not be in the least necessary to deal with the bridge at all and therefore they are in exactly the same position as the Lancashire Tramway Company were in the other House.

The Chairman : If that is 80 it seems to me we shall have t 9 hear the arguments on both sides and then come to our decision, but I do think it is hardly necsssary to call any evidence. Mr. Littler. I think I may shorten matters to a certain extent. Of course it they make a bridge my mouth is shut. I do not now discuss whether the tramway is wanted or not. They must judge for themselves whether it is good or bad, it is no business of mine : but if I am to share any part of the cost then I shall have to show you what the position of affairs is.
The Chairman: Are you going to call any witheasee or not?

Mr. Wedderburn : If my learned friend is going to contend that the tramway is net necessary I must call evidence. If, on the other band, it is simply to be a question of a clause as regards the cost of a bridge, then I think I could dispense with calling any witnesses. Mr. Littler: But you will pay for the cost of the bridge. •Mr Wedderburn : I will not. __ _ _ _

Mr. Littler : If you ;7-ill-paifo-r—t-h.e cost of the bridge. I have nothing to say as t? whethe: the tramway is necessary or not; hut if you say that you win not pay for the cost of the bridge then I say that there is no reason why you should have your tramway. The Chairman: But I understood Mr. Wedderbnrn is willing to pay for a portion of the bridge. Mr. Wedderburn : lam quite content to pay half. The Chairman : Then, Mr. Littler, in face of the committee's other decision I do not know what you have to say. _ _

Mr. Littler: If the tramway is utterly unnecessary there is no reason why we shout.] pay anything. Mr. Wedderburn : If my learned friend intends to go on, I shall ask you to say that the Railway Company should pay the lot. Mr. Littler : I am afraid it is a little too late for that. __

Mr Ernest Moon: You will renvimber, sir,that in the other case yea decided that the Railway Corupany were to pay for the whole cost of the bridge. and that is exactly what we are asking the promoters to do in this case.

Mr. Wcdderburn : Perhaps it might shorten it in this way—and lam anxious to shorten the proceedings if I can. Might I suggest this ? Ido not wish to say more than I ought to say but I Rather from what has fall"n from the committee that they are not averse to the clause as it stands, aryl if the committee thought fit I mignt reserve my evidenc:! and !et me see how far my learned friend Mr Littler can deal with the matter if he has got any evidence to call. Mr. Littler : No, no. The Chairman : I think, Mr. Wedderburn, you had better go on.

Majo—r Philip Cardew was called and said he was for merly in her Majesty's service in the Royal Engineers and 'ben for some ten years he was also electrical advis'r to the Board of Trade. He had now entered into pee- nership with Sir William Preece, and in conjo.action with him the matter of the construction of train ways in Warrington had come under his notice. He had pre- pared a scheme that was submitted to the C )rporation and of which this formed part. Warrington was and had always been known as a rather old-fashioned town and it was very difficult to lay out a scheme of tramways on account of the narrownesa of some of the streets. It was owing to the public spirit of the Corporation in widening these narrow streets that he had been able to devise this scheme. The scheme had been sanctioned by the Board of Trade subject to certain mcdifications and one of those modifications was a condition precedent with regard to the level crossing, that it should not be ; taken over the railway without tbe consent of the Board ! of Trade in writing. He had examined the proposed , crossing and, having regard to the way in which it was intended to construct the tramway and also to I, the level crossing he did not think it would affect the public safety provided that there were proper restric- tions put upon the traffic at that point. As Consulting Engineer to the Corporation be had advised them that ' certain restrictions would be necessary and he had no doubt that the Board of Trade would insist upon fired stops and a slow rate of speed in the vicinity. As regarded the cost of the bridge be was afraid it would be a very serious matter on account of the value of the property that would have to be acquired to make the approaches. The Railway Company had been enjoying the use of a portion of this road as a way-leave for some years. He did not think there was any reason why the right of use of the road by the public to an increased

A letter was received from the Warrington Trades and Labour Council suggesting the dePirability of forming a local Board of Conciliation, and asking the Chamber to receive a deputation to discuss the subject. The pro- posal was favourably received, but it was resolved to leave the matter over for further consideration at a fuller meeting.

div.head: WARRINGTON CORPORA-
div.p: WARRINGTON CORPORA-
TION TRAMWAYS.
The Order before the House
of Commons.

The Warrington Corporation Tramways Order Came before a Committee of the House of Commons on Monday. The chair was occupied by the Right Ron. Charles Seale-Bayne. Mr. Wedderburn, Q.C. and Mr. Hutchinson appeared as counsel on behalf of the Bill (instructed by Messrs. Baker, Lees and Company as agents). Mr. Pope, Q C., Mr Littler, , C.B., and Mr Ernest Moon appeared as counsel in support oi the petition of the London and North- Western Railway Company (instructed by Mr C H Mason as agent). The Town Clerk of Warrington Oar J Lyon Whittle)and the Borough Surveyor (Mr Longdin) and Major Philip Cardew were present as Witnesses in support of the order. Mr. Wedderburn in opening the case on behalf of the promoters of the Bill referred to an alteration Which had been made in the order whereby the Clause commencing "in the event of its becoming necessary in the opinion of the promoters that the road should be carried over the railway," should read thus "In the event of the Board of Trade at nay time hereafter making an order that the road hall be carried over the railway." Mr. Littler: That is to say you strike out down to the word " should," and then substitute for that the words "The Board of Trade at any time hereafter %airing an order that the road shall." Mr. Wedderburn : Yes, I dare say it may be that there are some additional matters that will have to be altered. Mr. Littler : The position is simply this,that of course the machinery for carrying out this question was not agreed by the commiVee,but I have no doubt my learned friend will agree upon it. This is all a part of the 'Principle in this sense that we have now agreed to in the Shape in which the Committee of the House of Lards Wished it to be. Mr. Wedderburn: That was the reason why I called attention to it, in order that the committee may get at absolutely what we are going to fight in the form where It is to be fought. Continuing, the learned counsel maid the town of Warrington was one of considerable Importance and also of considerable size. The Corpora- tion dated from the y,ar 1847, and the borough was extended in the year 1896, and had just become what yeas known as a'enunty borough. Its population in 1891 Was alreadv over 50,000, and it was cow estimated at acme 85,000 people. It was not unnatural that the developmpot of tramways in the borough should be a matter of eoniiiderable importance to it, and the result Was that the Corporation of Warrington themselves had aPplied for this order which they had obtained from the Board of Trade for the working of electrical traniwaVs. The Chairman : Is your tramway to be single or clouble? Mr. Weederburn. The tram wav,slr,will be double and Wilderspoal road already is a road along which there:is an immense amount of traffic.l am told that the pedestrians Who actually go along that road, and who cross that 'Point of the level crossir4g. number 7.000 a day,and that there are as many as 1,400 vehicles, and something over 400 'buses ; it is a road with slot of traffic. Mr. Littler : That is an error; one half of those 'buses go alone another road. Mr. Wedderburn: At any rate,if I have exaggerated 1 have done so unconsciously. Mr. Littler: The largest number is 163. _

quoted the Act of 1851 under which he said the rail wa, company were under a liability if the Board of Trad thought that the traffic and the Eafety of the public demanded it, to be ordered by the Board of Tr.de to build the bridge and to do away with the level crossing cairyin,g the road under or over the ailway at their sole expense. Further than that, under the Railway Clauqes Act of 1863, even apart from this private Act of 1851, section 7, there was practically the same provi- sion. _

Mr. Littler : That only applies to railways made after the year 1863; it does not apply to ours. Mr. Wedderburn : Chat very lik 457 may be so, and I am obliged to my learned friend for mentioning it,but the position is this, that the Act of 1851 makes quite clear what their position is. Further than that lam using this to show what the general principles of legis- lation are. Now then, sir, if you come to read this section, which has been put in by the other House, namely section 70, you will see that it is a section in relief of the Railway Company although they objet to it, because it says as you, the Corporation, are going to bring trams it is very likely that you are therefore going to hasten the time when the Railway Company would under the Act of 1851 at their own expense have to build a bridge, and we chin% the fair thing is that instead of paying as you would have to pay the whole of the cost, the Company should only pay half and the Corporation should pay half. The Company are not con- tent with that, and their suggestion has been that they should not contribute anything at all and that the thing should be carried out at the sole expense of the Cor- poration. The Chairman : Are you content with that? Mr. Wedderburn : Of course not ;it would be most unreasonable. _

The Chairman : But are you content wi, La the clause as it left the committee of the House of Lords ? Mr. Wodderburn : Yes, certainly. I think it is doing rather more for the company than ought to have been done, but I am quite content with it ; but that they should suggest that half the cost should be put noon thr, Corporation, and that they should contribute nothing is making a suggestion that is more crelitable to their courage than to their reasonableness. It is practically restricting the public right to use the road. Now, un- less my learned friend desires it I will not road his peti- tion. I have practically told you what it comes to. Mr. Littler: No, I do not think it is necewary to read it

—iir..-Wedderburs : Then, sir, the only other matter on that clause on page 90 is this : My learned friend Mr. Littler reminds me that they are going to put for- ward the case that this tramway and this road are not necessary. Of course, we shall give you evidence about that, and all about the traffic, and we shall submit that it is necessary. The Board of Tra le thought it necessary and the House of Loris thought it necessary, arid the people of Warrington know it is necessary, and tne only people who pretend that it is not, and want to k .ep the public out of this convenience for their own purposes are the London anl North-Western Railway Company. But I cannot help thinking that the very fact t iat they are driven to ailege that it is not necessary shows that they know if it is shown to iv necessary that they must con- tribute at least one-half towards the cost of the bridge Then, sir, the only other matter I would call your atten- tion to is this: I understood my learned friend Mr Littler to say that as regards that claueein case th Cor- poration shall construct such works as may be necessary for carrrinz the road over tne railway according to plans submitted to the L. and N..-W. Railway Company, there must be some arbitration in case of dispute. Mr. Littler : That is merely a matter of clime. I am Rot zninz to trouble the Committee with that now. I wanted to protect myself from its being supposed that I was content with this clause in detail.

COMMERCE. Meeting Of t—h—e Council.

A meeting of the Council was held at thn Market-gate Chambers on Monday. Mr John Fairclough occupied the chair. Messrs Fletcher, }Lomeli and Co., Limited, were unanimously elected members of thn Chamber.

div.head: ANNUAL CONGRESS
div.p: THE ANNUAL CONGRESS

The SECRETARY reported that, together with Mr. C. E Parker and Mr. William L ing, he attended the fourth Congress of the Ch ,mbers of Commerce of the Empire in London last month, a report of the proceedings of which had been communicated to the Pre3s by Mr. Parker.

div.head: SUGGESTED BOARD OF CONCILIATION.
div.p: SUGGESTED BOARD OF CONCILIATION.
THE COSPOR.ATION AND TEE SHIP CANAL.

Some discussion took place with reference to various matters in dispute between the Corporation and the Ship Canal Company, and it was resolved that the attention of the Council having been brought by members who are greatly interesttd in the navigatiom of the Mersey to the fact that the dredging is qlitn inadequate, and that it is impossible to use the river as intended until the Canal Company comply with their obligations under the act, the Secretary be requested to urge ttrm to give the matter their very serious consideration fotthwith.

The Chamber have received from the Philadelphia Commercial Museum an elaborate cabinet containing alphabetical particulars of the leading representatives of all the principal trades in the United States with a view to the promotion of mutual trade relations between the two countries. Information as to the principal importers and exporters of that country will be furnished to any person interested in the subject en application to the Secretary (Mr. Arthur Bennett).

div.head: SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT
div.p: SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT
AT ST. HELENS.
One Man Killed and Another Injured.

A most serious accident happened on Tuesday mora- ine at the Sherdley Colliery. belonging to the Whitecross Colliery Company, St Helens, when Thomas Crooks aged nineteen, a collier's drawer, of 17, Williamson-street, was killed instantly, and Ei ward Corrigan, aged forty-one a married man. of 1, Howell- street, Pocket Nook, '.as bully injured. Crooks was engaged as a drawer for his father, Joseph Crooks. After working all night, deceased pu-. on his clothes at half-past them, and followed his father out of the work- ing-pla•!*. The older Crooks had been gone out about , ten minutes. Deceased met Corrigan, and a man named Woodhead. in the down brew, where an endless rope is fixed for the haulage of boxes of coal. Carrigan iashed a couple of full boxes to the rope, and sigrmiled them away. The three m-n then walked along towards the pit shaft for home, when suddenly two of the full boxes, which had come loose from the haulage, dashed into Crooks, and killed him on the spo'. Corrigan Was also knocked down, and suffered a compound lractute of the left leg and other injuries, tot Woodhead jumped into a manhole by the aide of the road, and so escaped. I Corrigan Was taken t,l the St. Helens Hospital.
