The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet ending June 30, 1900, said tbe pod. tion and prospects of the bank continued to be satisfac tory. Irrespective of the business relating to the fsle of Man transactions awl the Ashton and Stalybrid,ge Bank, the number of accounts had increased in the ordinary business of the bank by over 2,400 during the last half year. With regard to the purchase of the business ot Dumb+)Ws Bank, the question might be asked— How came they as directors to ne 60 impru- dent as to buy a concern in liquidation. He dared say, as many present knew the dire tors, and bankers in particular, had reason to know that every concern had a breaking up value, and they believed that,, in making their offer of £40,000, zonditionally on having the premises secure) to them alse,at the very reasonat:ee price of £15,000. so that they would be on the spet.they would not only do a very Food stroke of business for themselves eventually, but also for the shareholders and the depositors of Dumbeira Bank, by promptly coming to the rescue in what was a very serious business indeed. He was glad to say that their belief had been already justified, fo: the amount of depo:its which returning confidence had placed in their hands, and continued to place week by we: k, already ensured a very fair return upon tneir outlay. The number of accounts c natinued to mount up at the rate of 30 or 40 a week. (Uear, hear.) He timue `cat without undue vanity, they might take some credit to themselves for deservine that confidence, for they endeavoured to meets very sarious situation in a broad- minded and liberal spirit,and they hoped consieent with their duty to their own shareholders. That duty forbade them to carry out the original scheme of amalgamation, which had been proposed, and subsequent disclosures, as the meeting knew, more than justified that refusal. They at once. however, did what they could ta mitigate and did materially mitigate, the severity of the crisis and avert widespread disaster in the island. They promptly sent over clerks, and gold, and at once announced their intention to advance 103. in the pound to the depositors in the bank. Though the directors of Parr's Beak might run some risk of blame from their own share- holders there could be but one ()pinion as to the happy effect their action bad had warn the financial stability of the Isle of Man. Their action had been more than justified from a selfish point of view. Referring to the proposal as to the creation and issue of 4,675 shares, and the transfer to Pared Bank of the business and premises of the Ashton and Stalybridge Bank, which had bean confirmed at the meeting just bold, the Chairman said that hank was an old-established ~ concern doing a sound business in a district which was part of what he might call "greater Manchester," where their own bank already had a large and important business. After devoting 1.250 of the new shares to that purchase, there remained a balance of 3,425 shares, which provided for one new share for every twenty shares already held, and they would be offered in that proportion to the old shareholders who were Oa the register on the 18th July. Taking the market price of that share at £9O it gave the old ehareholderi a bonus of exactly £1 per share. The effect of the operation would be to raise the subscribed capital to £7,317,500. and the pail up Capital, by the sum of £93,500, to £1.463,500. The premium of £59 per share to tee paid upon time 3,425 shares to be allotted to their own nhareholdo rs would produce the eum of £171,250. That sum they desired, with the permission of the meeting, to apply as follows :—To reeerve fund, £68,500; to clear off the SUM of £40,000 paid for the business of Dumbell's Bank, with interest thereon, £40,293; and to the bank premises account £62,457 After that day he was glad to say they would see nothing in future reports to remind them of the unfortunate epiaode of the stolen notes. Practically all the notes of the £60,000 originally stolen had bean recovered, and they were perhaps more fortunate than they could possibly have hoped to be. In June of last year they trespassed on the account t arried forward to tbe extent of £20,610 in respect of possible loss on those notes. They now deducted the sum of £2,610 which they retained for legal and other sap -rises, and possible loss on a few notes that were still outstanding in the hands of 'somebody, and they asked to be allowed to retransfer £lB,OOO, making the total balance to be carried to next account £94,329. Having referred to other items in the balar c -sheet, the Chairman said that in the autumn of last year they were all looking forward to a general extension of trade,which had been unparalleled since 1870, in spite of our task in South Africa, which had proved greater in magnitude and longer in disration than most people apprehended at the outset, and other disqlieting circumstances. Though trade was still good, there was rot wanting signs which prudent men would not oisregard as to the chances of a cetionuance of brisk trade. The prices of several leading commodities were not at the high figure which prevailed in the, early months of this year. On the other hand, eeal was still dear enough to materially check the flow of manufacturing enterprise, and so much money had been spent and atilt would be anant in unprofitable labour on war and war material for South Africa and elsewhere that there must be a corree-

ponding loss of expenditure on the ordinary products of consuo.ption both ia Great Britain and the colonies The lavish though neceseary expenditure to which h., had referred must make itself felt more acutely later ou than at present. When, however, our troubles were over and South Africa and other countries were thrown open Ito the trade of the world to a far greater extent than ever before, he hoped England might possibly see a boom in trade which might even dwarf the expectations of the most sanguine amongst them, but that time was not yet.

On Sunday Home Mission anniversary services were held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, when the preacher morning and evening was the REV. James E. Hargreaves. Collections were taken in aid of the mis- sionss—On Monday evening a public meeting was held in the chapel. The Rev. T. Bishop presiding in the unavoidable absence of Dr. R E. Harcourt. After devo- tional exercises the Chairman explained that the absenee• of Dr. Harcourt was due to the death of a relation. He went on to report', as the secretary pro tern., that the ordinary income of the Homo Mission Society frcm subscriptions and collections and the Juvenile Association last year amounted to £25,884 78 9d and the entire income of the fund from all sources was £35,976, while the expenses were £36,296. showing a deficiency of nearly £320. The utmost care on the part ot those who administered the funds of the society had not resuked in keepine them entirely free from debt, but he did not himself think that the debt was a great incubus. A debt of that kind was sometimes a stimulus to more generous giving. There was no fund in all Methodism which did more good or made 20s go further in the pound than this fund did. The report showed them that everywhere where home missionary affairs were in operation there wee success. He wou'd read the first line under the various headings in the re- pert- In special mission to fishermen in the North Sea it began "One more success can be reported in the work," the next" A year of ucprecedented blessings,"" A year of success, op eortunity,s,nd crippled fun's," and "Never was the spiritual tone deeper nor its energies more active, never have members been more firm than at the present moment." All the way through there was just the same tone running, that note of suppressed triumph mingled with gratitude and hope. The income of the society was made up from several sources,first of which were the collections made in the chapels, and these with subscriptions amounted to £23,361. Then there were the yearly collections, and then there were legacies occasionally. In ad- dition there was what was collected by the young people. As regarded the expenditure, there were cir- cuits throughout the country not strong enough to sup- port their ministers. Ministers were not like angels. They could not live on nothing. (Laughter.) There were groups of villages and small country towns which could not scrape enough together to support a minister, and they had.to be helped from this fund. The amount expended this way was £9,688. Then there were extra- ordinary grants which amounted to £8,355, and con- nexional expsnses £3,500 They had no endowments, they were a volts tary church, and they thanked God for it. They helped one another to bear one another's burdens. They had chaplains in the army, and also supported the Seamen's Mission and the Shorerlitch Mission. The report told them of lives rescued from misery and shame and brought to the means of earning a good and honest livelihood. He appealed to them to help a mission which was doing such work. The Rev. J. E. HARGREAVES delivered an address on " Tbe Progress and development of the Wesleyan Home Missions." He said that the contingent expenses fund would in future be separate from the general fund. The home missien work was in the first instant joined to the contingent fund, which was one of the oldest funds they had got. The progress of the home mission move- ment had so advanced that the two would in future be sen4rate. Mr. Bishop had spoken to them of a debt of I £3OO, hut it was not really a debt. It could be wiped off at any moment they cared to do it. The fact was that they had received as much as they ought to have done. He was afraid there was a lack of interest, but he hoped the new legislation would create a quickened interest in their home mission work. He was thankful for the interest that was taken by the Methodist people in their foreign missionary work. They must not for- get, however, that there were people around them who needed the Gospel as much as the people abroad. It was 44 years since the home missionary movement started, and its development was remarkable Be had worked in Carlisle. Sunderland,the Shetland Islandreand th east end of London, and although for many years engaged in purely circuit work had always been asso- ciated with the mission movement by being a member of the general committee. He described the work of the various missions, and in the relation of his own experi- ence, traced the development of the movement. At the close a collection was taken in aid of the missions.

div.head: Speech by the Chairman.
div.p: Speech by the Chairman.
OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel.
Gospel Hall.

On Sunday, Mr. W. Beesley, of Bolton preached from the 3rd of Acts. affirming that the cure of the lame man at the Temple Gate by Peter and John using the name of Jesus was a positive proof of the resurrection and glorification of Christ. He WAS put to death in weak- -,ess but raivd again with power and a name given to Him which is above every name. God used this miracle so as to give an opportunity to Peter and John to testify for Christ and the first thing they did was to bring home to the people their awful sin in murdering the Son of God. The Holy Spirit to-day is convicting men of the terrible sin of rejecting the Son of God. If people could only realise then their sinful state before God we should see more sound conversions. There is still power in filename of Jesus, for in His name is preached for- giveness of sin and the justification from all thing.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

At the meeting of this S,ciety on Sunday. the chair was occupied by Mr. George Wallington. The address for the afternoon was delivered by Mr. William Silcock. who greatly interested his hearers by an eloquent appeal for the careful training and up-bringing of children. He showed how important it was that child life should be surrounded by the best influ.nces.—The Chairman added a few words on the same subject.—The service was also taken part in by Mr. B. Farrar, the hon. secretary, Mr. William Beswick, and Mr. William Beswick, junior.
- End of the Strike of Harvestmen.

The farmers in the district of Hartford, Weaver- ham, Acton, and Sandiway affected by the recent strike of Irish harvestmen assembled at the Crown and Anchor Hotel, Nerthivich, on Saturday morn- ng for the purpose of having a conference with Mr. P Flannery, who was acting as mediator.—Mr. J Cross occupied the chair. Mr. Flannery explained to the farmers that the mon wanted 188 a week with bagging, and a bonus at the end of the harvest. To this the farmers stoutly refused to agree, but after a lengthy consultation decided to partially meet the men by giving thPrn 17s a week with beer, bagging. and .EI harvest bonus, or as an alternative 188 weekly with bagging and bonus. The decision of the masters was communicated to the men, and whilst some appeared perfectly satisfied others threatened to remain out until the masters acceded to their demands. Upon the masters being informed of this,they threatened to prosecute those men who assembled in gangs and visited farms for the pur- pose of fetching men out who were willing to work. On Monday nearly all the men had returned to work on the terms offered by the masters. Sunday School Teachers' Association.

The quarterly meeting of the Warrington and District Sunday School Teachers' Association was held at the Rectory on Saturday afternoon. The members met at three o'clock and indulged in various games until half-past five, when tea was partaken of in the Fairfield schools. A service was held in the Parish Church when an address of a spiritual character was given by the Rev. H. Gibson Smith, rector of Halewood. The service over, the members adjourned to the Rectory gardens and again amused themselves until dusk.

div.p: WARRINGTON.

Warrington and the Death of the Duke of Saxe-Coburg. Flags at the Town Hall and at other places were hoisted at half-mast on Tuesday morning as soon as the news of the death of the Queen's second son was received.

div.head: Warrington Clergy Charities.
div.p: The Warrington Clergy Charities.

At Holy Trinity Church on gu'uday morning and evening, the offertory, which amounted to £3 168, was devoted to the Warrington Clergy Charities. Coming Events. The Warrington Football Club- Amateur Athletic Sports will be held on the football ground, Wilder- spool-road, on Monday (Bank Holiday). Valuable prizes,which have been supplied by Messrs.Bustance and Co., of Sankey-street, and may be seen in the .hop window of Messrs. Dolan Bros., will be com- peted for. Catholic Association.

On Saturday, the members of the above Associa- tion, which was formed last October, and has a membership of 300, held their first annual excur- sion. The place selected was Eastham, the Rich- mond of the Mersey. The party numbered upwards of WO, and included the clergy and several of the leading Roman Catholics of tbe town. Tea was provided in the Gardens, where amusements were indulged in, and after an enjoyable outing the party returned to Warrington about ten o'clock. The arrangements were carried out by the Secretary, Mr James Mather.

div.head: Presentation to Mr. Isaac Hayward.
div.p: Presentation to Mr. Isaac Hayward.

On Sunday evening a presentation took place at Bold-street Wesleyan Cnapel to Mr. Isaac Hayward, who was for many years one of the foremen of White Cross Works, and has left Warrington to un- dertake a similar position at Wakefield. He has been a member of the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Churn for 27 years, and for four years was society steward. The presentation took place in the steward's vestry after service, and was made on be- half of the congregation by the Rev. T. Bishop. The gifts were a silver tea kettle and spirit lamp and a silver biscuit barrel. There was a representa- tive uttecidaucu of members of the congregation.and several speeches were delivered.—Mr Place said he felt his position very acutely. Mr. Hayward had been a friend of his for over thirty years, and he had always proved himself to be a Christian. , (Hear, hear) They had lost many friends during the last few years. He (the speaker) hoped God's blessing would go with .Mr. Hayward in his new sphere of labour.—Mr. Davey said that to part with Mr. Hayward was like severing a limb. It had been his privilege to work with him as society steward, and he looked upon the times thus spent together as the happiest in his life. In wishing Mr. Hayward "God-speed " he could only say that Warrington's loss was Wakefield's gain.—Ml‘. Isaac Johnson regarded Mr. Hayward as a dear friend. They had known one another for many years and bad met at the " class " meetings. He hoped he would be a blessing to those with "'''whom he came into contact —Mr. Norman, Mr. Taylor, and the Rev.. Theodore Bishop also addressed the meeting, and in a few well chosen words, the latter presented the kettle and biscuit barrel. He said Mr. Hayward would he very much missed in the church, and it would not be easy to replace a man of his experience. The present was small compared with the love and affection it represented. It w‘-auld,. however, help to soften the pang of parting from them.—Mr. Hay- ward, who was deeply affected, returned thanks. So many kind words had been said of him during the last few days that he Could not believe them all, but he would not forget his 27 Nears' connection with the chapel or the many kind friends be had left behind him. Someone had said: "Be pitiful, every man has a battle to fight"; that was so. He loved his daily work and his whole heart was in it. He belonged to the third or fourth generation of the family. He believed Bewsey-road Church would be a more prosperous church in the future than it bad ever been. He thanked all very sincerely for the kind expressions which had been used with re- gard to him.

THE relief on hearing that the, The Truce at Pekin. foreign Ministers at Pekin

have hitherto escaped mas- sacre, though they are still besieged in the Legations, is so considerable that there is a tendency to underestimate the gravity of the situation. What has been arranged is a kind of truce. The small force in the Legations,which has been materially reduced by the siege, has been vigorously attacking the investors, and has been requested to desist from its attacks. A cordon Of Chinese soldiers hes been placed between the Legations and the Boxers, and so far all is well • Probably provisions may be allowed to paso through. It is now quite evident that an attempt has been made to use the Ministers and refugees as hostages, and to make terms as the price of their safety. We take this to be the aim Of Li HIINCI OHANG's mission. He has ni with so much discouragement that he is un- willing to go to Pekin, and he recommends the EMPRESS to send the Ministers under safe escort to Tientsin, and to prevent at all costs the murder of missionaries and converts. His foreaer threat, that the Ministers would be murdered If the Allied troops advanced on Pekin, has been abandoned, and we may infer that a pause has occurred, in which there is some confusion In Chinese counsels. The fall of Tientsin and the arrival of more troops has induced the ENcrEzos ts exert herself and to shew some authority where there had been complete passivity and indifference before. There are some Chinese Christians in the cathedral at Pekin, and they have been holdingent against the Boxers, though they could hardly have done so if the Chinese troops had been helping the insurgents as they did in the first instance. Thor° is now a fear on the part of the Boxers that theY may be caught between two fires—attacked .bY the Chinese troops and attacked by the Allies They have heard of the capture of Tientsi° and the severe losses of their comrades in It 3 defence. They are wavering. We hope they will continue to waver, and end by being Paci.u,e. But we cannot say what may happen outsif Pekin when the Allies advance, or what DlaY 1E43 the mood of the revolutionists in the city Whet) they see the" foreign devils " coming along, NI armed, to Finish them for their misdeeds, Itt. ne may fear inquiry, and they may once more Pre`—i to fight, aid do their hest to influence a par . the Chinese troops to throw in their lot with thee:l" Until the foreign ministers are either safe I'l Tientsin or actually rescued by the Allies vie shall be wrong to take a placid view of tliel situation. The Chinese character forbids loVes explanation. The hope is, however, that 00 EMPRESS and her advisers may be thoroughly esir vinced of the imperative importance of resisto% the revolution, of trying to save the dynasty/ $ll4 of rendering what assistance they can in the Os' toration of order and peace. The Cainese ars° is sn awkward factor in the situation. Where PRINCE TITAN is we do not know, and whether 12° has been substantially reinforced or not cannot 130 ascertained. Happily, the Ministers are alive, htlt' beyond that all is dark and uncertain. 0111 advance from Tientsin should not now be log delayed.

THE heart of Engls)24 The Duke of Saxe- has received another Coburg and Gotha. shock. It is some 3sisrsA since a breach was made in the Rayal Family our beloved OMEN was called upon to remember that she is not exempt from the sorrow and eels's" ity that assail ordinary human beings. Yesterds/ she heard with pain and grief ef the death of 0,11 Duke of SAXE-COBURG and GOTHA from paralY6l6 of the heart. He had been ailing for some tiele' and he had made several visits to health resorts t° improve his condition, with but partial bensti°' But it was not thought that he was in any danger of sudden death, as far as our knowledge in thi° country went, though it is possible he and Olt/ DUCHESS had been warned of the weakness ° which he succumbed at Rosenau Castle on lite°l- day night. Be that as it may, there will be gaol, grief in England and in his Duchy, and rase.,l sympathy for our venerable QUEEN, who 111114 probably feel this blow more than the others whic' have preceded it. The Duke of EDINBURGH a° Wl° still call him, had had an eventful career, and had had the fate ot many Royal personages 11 being assailed by an assassin. O'Farrell, wounded him in the back at a picnic at Clontarf New South Wales was generally believed to been a Fenian. The horror the deed excited universal. It will probably belreasembered by middle-aged that the late Duke was at one tirsa: more popular than the PUINCE of WALES. Lb 9r7i always spoken of with affection, and it was 5411 that he had been gifted with greater natal.: intelligence. His connection with the navy pr(; ably had something to do with his poptliarit"; Mixing more freely with others, he travelled td various parts of the world, and worthily sustiitls the position he held in the Royal Family. form and figure were well known in every her M4jesty's wide dominion. As a naval eigg and a ROYAL PRINCE he was heartily welcesl.o, everywhere. In 1874 he married the ag'it'er DUCHESS MARIE ALEXANDROVNA,tiIe only dale cv of the CZAR ALEXANDER 11. It would be inc°7l st to say that this marriage waa as popular as 'to contracted by the PRINCE of WALES. It led d questions about precedence, and, it is believe the bestowal on the QUEEN of the title of Dirs:iier of INDIA, the better to secure the rank of her

children and their offspring. However no harm bas come from the union, and the DUCHESS Of SAXE-COBURG and GOTHA Will receive, irt her great bereavemeut, the tenderest sTropathy of the English people. Her posi- tion is now one of peculiar delicacy. Bereft of a son to inherit the position of Grand Duke—a great sorrow to her and the late Duke— the Du,2hy will pass into the care of the Prince of ROHENLOHE-LANGENBURG until the DUKE of ALBANY is of age. The feeling in this country over the death of PRINCE ALFRED will be one of great sorrow. Ho was attached to this country, though he had ceased to reside here, and he was always welcome on his annual visits, which were the brightest part of his life. As ruler, father,aud Wond son of the QUEEN, he had filled a conspicu- ous position with rare ability and zeal. The PRINCE of WALES and he were the most attached Of brothers. Daring the PRINCE of WALES'S ill- ness he was always cheerful and confident of the PRINCE'S recovery. A little anecdote was current rnany years ago that illustrates their relation to each other. "It is a good job for me," the PRINCE of WALES is reported to have said, "that the next King of England is not to be elected on the competitive examination system, or I should Stand a poor chance against you." To lose such a brother must be a groat grief to the PB.INCE. How flinch more must it be a loss to our beloved and aged QUEEN ! May she have strength to bear the burden!

The picture sales at the Royal Academy this season are found to have been up to the average, though 1:4,000 below the exceptionally good return of last year. The smaller canvases have done Particularly well, which is a hint to artists to re- member the difficulties of hanging in private houses. It is noteworthy, too, that in the" Daily News" plebiwite of the best pictures of the year the honour in respect of ' the picture you would like best t 3 live with" goes to Mr. Alma Tadema for his miniature of gold fish, SO beautifully drawn and so exquisitely iridescent. Mr. Sargent's Portrait of Lord Russell of Killowen is adjudged in the same competition the best of its kind ; while the khaki feeling makes itself evident in the Opinion that Lord Kitchener comes out on canvas the best-looking man. Were it "under canvas there would be no disputing the point, but several faces have richer expression without deficiency of Will power, which gives the General his attractive- ness. There are, however, at Burlington House far too many portraits of ordinary people, who seem to imagine that this way lies fame, whereas 411 they get is notoriety and criticism. Still, they help to fill the purses of the artists, and whatever landscapes and seascapes may have to be taken to the dealers at the close of the exhibition, to be realised as well as may be, the portraits are taken to the homes and proudly displayed. The poor have to be content with enlarged photographs in the Sunday sitting-room; but while both classes humour themselves in this way, who shall say we are not an artistic nation? How wicked it is of Sir W. B. Richmond to suggest, as he has done lately that there is something lacking.

It is part of the scheme of the Government for the maintenance of peace in South Africa that 1;5,000 of the soldiers should be induced to settle lo the country as colonists. The supposition has been that not a few of these would consist of Australian and New Zealand troopers, who, in a Peculiar degree, are trained agriculturists, and Nplendid sportsmen as well. The premier of New Zealand, however, has anticipated this action by a protest. Neither New Zealand nor Australia can afford to spare permanently men who are their best and most useful types ; and it is probable that our Government will have to restrict its offer, whenever formulated, to soldiers coming ftrorn our own country. It would be a poor return the enthusiastic genensity which prompted is'u.cl aid of these auxiliary forces if we were to '''naPt them to remain in the new land, when the Agents-General for the Colonies are issuing aPPeals to able-bodied emigrants. The colonial soldiers themselves may be somewhat annoyed if they are debarred from taking up some of these grants to be made, but they have been paid at special rates, and that should be a consolation to them. The suggestion, however, that the Imperial Government should insist on their return to Australasia by withholding a great part of their remuneration is absurd. If they want to settle in South Africa they must be free to do so, of their own volition.

We have had bad news and good in plenty this week, but unfortunately the former predominates in importance over the latter. On Monday the civilised world was shocked and sickened by the assassination of King Humbert, the victim of a sen,seless Tusean Anarchist. The King of Italy Was one of the last monarchs whom we should have thought even Anarchists would wish to re- move. We agree with Mr. Labouchere that Persons who seek to kill kings and queens merely because of their royalty ought all to be condemned to death. A common Murderer, with may-be a strong motive as excuse is promptly executed, and it is criminal leniency to do other than make these Anarchists suffer the lull penalty of their crime. The King of Italy's tragic end created a profound sonsation,from which the people of this country had not recovered when the news came of the Duke of Edinburgh's death at a lamentably early age. Her Majesty has the full sympathy of her people in the sad loss she has sustained by the death of her second son. Per good news we gladly turn to China, where our hearts have been held in suspense so long. The 'misters in Pekin are safe, there is good reason to believe' and Europe rejoices greatly thereat. From South Africa too, come tidings of important suc- cesses byHunter and Hamilton,who have compelled two or three thousand Boers to surrender. There has indeed been asurfeit of news this week, and a Period of quietness and peace would not be Unwelcome.

What is becoming familiarly known JIB "the Thelwall nuisance" progressed another stage further at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural Council on Tuesday, when Dr. Adams submitted an analysis of effluents from the Tannery and from the brook at a point lower down. Neither were good, but that from the Tannery was described as very bad and contributing materially to the nuis- ance. Messrs. Long and Son will therefore have tO join Mr. Naylor in the purification of the stream which the latter styles a " veritable death- trap." Between them and the District Council the brook should be carefully looked after in future. "Ilrein the correspondence which has passed it Would seem that Messrs. Naylor and Long each looked suspiciously on the other in this matter of contamination, and the proven guilt of both pro- vokes not a little arnu.sement in the minds of urn- Partial and disinterested observers.

The Warrington Tramways Order has been 41)Proved by a Committee of the House of Corn- teons this week and its confirmation has been °Perted to the House. The only opponents to the „%aill were the London and North-Western Railway uerripany and they failed completely in their endeavour to get out of the obligation imposed 4113e0 them by the House of Lords to pay half the eeet of the construction of a bridge across the rail- at Wilderspool in the event of one being erdered by the Board of Trade. The counsel for the railway company referred to the position which the Company had taken up in this matter 4k a comprehensible one, but the Committee did Let exact!), view the case in that light. On the I),t,her hand, the Chairman cf the Committee "Italy stated that the Railway Company had !c't off extremely well. This will be the ki.Tneral opinion of the ratepayers of War- t: gton, especially when it is borne in ielnd that in the Act of 1851, when the present ,jel crossing was sanctioned, it was expressly IPulated that if the traffic on the road became of 811cha -lake it undesirable that there

should be a level crossing at Wilderspool Cause- way, it would be open to the Board of Trade to say that the railway company must either carry their line over the road or carry the road at their own expense over the line.

The proposed electric tramway has no doubt hastened matters, but in the natural course of things, the congestion of traffic at this point must have forced the railway company to provide a bridge within a few years. The Warrington Cor- poration have now been ordered to help them in the cost to the extent of one half, and then with base ingratitude the Railway Company petition the Committee to order the Corporation to pay the whole cost. For unblushing impudence and avarice commend us to a railway company. 1110179

The London and North-Western Riilway Com- pany seem determined to oppose the Warrington Corporation Tramways Order to the bitter end. One would have thought that the decision of the House of Lords" Committee would at least have I, satisfied them, for the conditions laid down cannot by any stretch of the imagination be considered harsh on the railway company. It will be remembered that the committee ordered that in the event of the Board of Trade deciding that a bridge shall be constructed across the rail- way near Wilderspool crossing in the interests of the public safety, the cost must be defrayed in equal proportions by the railway company and the Corporation. The order is to come before a com- mittee of the House of Commons for confirmation this week, and the Railway Company have again lodged a petition against it. The Company contend in their petition that the whole cost ought to be defrayed by the Corporation,and we presume that they will endeavour to convince the House of Commons committee that such is a fair solution of the difficulty. How they will do so is not altogether clear. It seems difficult to believe that the committee will interfere with the decision of the House of Lords on such a flimsy pretext as that advanced in this case.

There seems to be a boom in local Conservatism just now, which is attributable, we suppose,like so many other unexpected things, to the war. What a lot this Savage South African conflict is going to be responsible for! It has already ruined a number of reputations, cost thousands of lives, expended millions of money, and contributed to a spread of the virulent poison of Conservatism. There are antidotes to most poisons, and it will not be long before there is one found for the latter. The Tory boom just re- ferred to has brought into existence a new club '• down Orford way '' which was opened with immense eclat last week. All the Conservative big guns of the district were exploded, mostly with blank cartridge, and the damage done to the other side was infinitesimal. Previous Govern- ments formed the principal target and on their shoulders was laid the responsibility for our pre- sent troubles, and also for many of the mistakes ot the present Government. The general election was welcomed in anticipation. Mr. Pierpoint spoke authoritatively to that effect that "if it was not this year it would be next" while Lord Newton was of the opinion that the more incon- venient it would be for the half of the country which was not Conservative, and the more reason it was that the election should be soon. The khaki vote,was not mentioned specifically, but the two M.P.'s expressed a leaning towards something of the kind which was quite significant.

Anyone who knows anything of the history of Warrington and neighbourhood is aware of the antiquity of Hill Cliffe Chapel. There is, however, a lack of definite information respecting the origin of this historic meeting place and the prob- able date of its foundation. The haziness which has surrounded its history for so long has been lifted somewhat within recent years by the in- vestigations which have been made by Mr. James Kenworthy and the Rev. J. S. Hughes. But much remains to be cleared up and this was exemplified by the excellent paper :read by the Pastor of the Chapel last week before a gathering of Liverpool Baptists who came on a pilgrimage to the historic shrine in connection with their bi-centenary celebra- tions. There appears tR be irrefragablo proof that Hill Cliffe is a pre-Reformation Ohurch,despite the sceptism of some antiquarians. That it has been in existenc) for three centuries seems indis- putable on the evidence now adduced, but to go beyond that date is somewhat in the nature of speculation. It is a singular fact that despite its interesting history, Hill Cliff() has been left severely alone by historians. In Ormerod's com- prehensive history of Cheshire, for instance, we behove no mention is to be found of Hill Cliffe, although a neighbouring church of a much more recent date is referred to. The same remark applies to some other local histories. It is eminently desirable that the truth should be known about Hill Clifte and in taking steps to unravel the mysteries associated with its history, the Baptists are showing a praiseworthy loyalty to their denomination, and performing a duty they owe to the public generally.

We thought Councillor Bennett held a position of +splendid isolation as a dreamer, but no! there is a rival in the field. The worthy Councillor is Lot to have the monopoly of forecasting the future in such roseate hues, for the pastor of Hill Cliffs Chapel has ventured boldly into the seine field of imagination. His method of procedure when on dreaming bent differs somewhat from that of the Councillor, for he tells us that he awoke first and dreamed afterwards. There is no recognised rule to go by, so it may not inatter,and in any case the result is the same. Mr. Hughes found instead of his modest little chapel, a stately structure in modern style with a dash of " ancient Greece " capital G please—about it. There were massive columns, graceful arches, alcoves and traceried windows, and all the other paraphernalia of a first-class dreamy edifice. Nothing seemed wanting, and when we found that Mr. Hughes had preached "well enough to wake the dead" around him—but unsuccessfully of course—we decided at once that his dream was quite up to the standard set by his predecessor Councillor Bennett. Both are very accomplished and while they live, ideas—valuablo ideas—for the future should not be lacking.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

It is curious to observe the process by which writers in the papers this week,on the assassination of King Humbert. gradually descend from high politics and the discussion of affairs of State, to speculating upon the possible effect which the in- famous deed may have upon the fortunes of the Paris Exhibition and the prospects of English people who have proposed to visit it. It appears from the statements of some of these writers that the Exhibition has already suffered somewhat in consequence of the attack upon the Prince of W9le9 some months ago at Brussels, and now that Anarchism has raised its hideous head again, the Prince is considerately urged to change his mind if he has had any intention of going there. Mean- while, no one seems really to know whether the Prince of Wales ever had any such intention, or whether he will go now. So far as many of the middle class people in the provinces who spoke enthusiastically two years ago about going to see Paris again are concerned, they are not quite so effervescent over the matter. Many things have happened in the two years, including the Dreyfus affair and the South African war, and the latter especially accounts for much of the supposed in- difference of the i..nglish towards Paris and her Ex- hibition.

Fifty years ago on Monday last, the Act. of Parlia- ment regulating libraries and museums was nased, and received th, Royal Assent a little later. Mr William Ewart.,a frierd ni the Gladstone familv,after whom the future Prime Minister and eminent Briti,,h sWesman was chri,tea.A, itti% iated the m )vement. which met with much opposition at the outset. A Colonel Sibthorp, wno ‘)pposed it vigorously, said the promoters of the Bill would next be " thinking of supplying the working classes with quoits, peg- tops, and footballs.' Opposition in Parliament, however, was gradually beatql down, and Mr Ewart had the satisfaction of both seeing the Bill become law and in auccesetul operation after.

! Its growth has been enormous during the half century, and it might well be asked wh re many of the provincial towns wouli ba now if it were not . for that enacr,ment ? It is estimated that the free public libraries in this country contain a total of about six million books. To the provinces, the i library movement is seclind in importance to that of 1 our national system of education.

Much appears to be expected from the round- table conference which the Bishop of Lnudon is promoting, with a view to establishing peace be- tween the various parties in the Anglican com- munion. His lords-tip is convinced that existing "religious quarrels "result mainly from the differ- ence of verbal expression or imperfect definition, and has selected representatives from each section, who will meet in the early autumn to discuss con- troverted points and remove mutual misunder- standings. This is very similar in effect to what his Grace of Canterbury said in the HouAn of Lords recently. If the minor clergy were of the same mind as the Archbishop and at least some of the Bishops, the matter would no doubt soon be put at rest, at least for a time; qnd there would be more peace at home, and between families and communi- ties, as well as in the churches, if the" representa- tives of each section" would meet as suggested, and would discuss " controverted points," instead of holding aloof from each other on various pretexts in the way they have done hitherto. Without a little of the worldly 'give and take "idea being admitted into the deliberations at the round-table, their efforts are not likely to do much good, and there has been small evidence of the existence of this kind of principle on other occasions.

Mr. E. T. Parker, St. Stephen's-street, Bristol, has offered to supply tree to any carter, costermouger, or others in his own city whose horses are for hours daily exposed to the present solar heat, a sun bonnet specially designed. This is not an adver- tisement. He simply wishes other lovers of horses, in country districts especially, to do something similar.

Of the truth that "the law is an ass" we are often reminded; but it must be one and the same cynic who this week points out that the Meteorological Office by its new scheme of supplying weaf.her tips at a penny each, and the proprietors of motor cars who employ a man or boy to clean the machine bring themselves within its meshes. He argues,of course, that it being illegal to run a game of chance for profit, makes the investment of a penny with the Meteorological Office the same kind of off tice. As there are finer points argued in our law courts than this appears to be,possibly the suggestion may yet find work for the lawyers; but the question raised in the motor car idea appears a little too fine for anything. How can the owner of the car be made subject to a male servant's license. The latter cannot be described as a " stable boy " within the meaning of the Act, seeing he has neither horses or stables to look after. But, as "Land and Water" says, it seems as if automobilists were to be cangPered a lawful prey for everyone who cares to pounce upon them: It was so with the cyclists for a time, but " wheelers " have so far lived down or 'run " down public antagonism that now they are in many parts of the country allowed to ju,t go as they please, and there is no question about their "going," as many elderly people often and plainly testify.

The distinction and the diff4rence between "law" and justice will be once more exemplified in this "liberty " loving land of ours if the prosecutors in a case which came before the Bolton magistracy the other day can have their way. A large and well- known firm of cotton manufacturers had employed a boy under twelve years of age and thereby in- fringed upon the recent Hobson enactment. But it was shown that the boy was profitably employed in helping to maintain pocr mother threatened with blindness, and on this plea the magistra' es dismissed the case. This was, but just, the reader will say, or" justice." But the law steps in, de- mands its " full pound of flesh," and gives notice of appeal ! Is it any wonder that it is so difficult to get measures passed on the mere ground of being calculated to prove highly advantageous and bene- ficial, when members of Parliament know how apt they sometimes are, unless safe guarded so as to make them almost valueless, to be abused by stick- lers for " the law and the letter?" Better that a nearly blind mother and dutiful son should be thrown on the rates,than that the law should under any circumstances be disregarded, argue the legal Shylocks ; but it is not easy to perceive where the justice comes in.

To the hot weather and the extent to which bathing prevails is due the circumstance of the question now being raised of how much more value in the eye of the law a dead body is than a living one. Anyhow, that is so in some places, and there are local authorities, including the Thames autho- rity at present considering the propriety of offering rewards for the recovery of dead bcdies. Yet the fact remains that there is no law in operation any- where in England to enforce compensation for the recovery of would-be suicides, or bathers seized with cramp, for instance. It is well for the latter that persons who rush to the rescue are just the last people in the world to think of compensation.

A clergyman, who has had twenty years' experi- ence of village parishes, wishes it to be asked where some of the sanitary authorities are? He adds that in the numerous important parishes of which he has knowledge, and where, if they have thriven it has been in spite of rather than by the help of these authorities, the conditions remain absolutely unaltered. There is good reason to believe, and know, that n.any of the things he says about them are applicable to others all over the country. After giving certain particulars, the vicar says the "property" would rally have to be seen by people who do not live in villages, to be "appreciated." It is not to ba wondered at, that the infant mortality of country districts reaches the abnormal figure of 42 per cent of the total, as against the Registrar- General's figures of 25 per cent for the whole coun- try. It is the opposite of creditable to the owners of such property, and the question needs to be asked: Where are the Sani•,ary Authorities ?

The Cottage Hospital Fund is to be further a,sis- teri by another excellent effort on the part of the Runcorn Cycle Club and their friends. What this club has thme in the past, the Runcorn public well know, and when they realise that the Cottage Hos- pital Fund now totals over .E6OO, they can take pride in it and congratulate themselves upon having a hand In a truly humanitarian work. In addition to its usefulness in promoting the Cottage Hospital Fund, the cycle parade has afforded a considerable amount of amusement to the inhabitants of the town, and has pleasured the dullness of many a day which would otherwise have been but commonplace and dreary.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT

Tee Runcorn Rural District Council are evidently surprised that their surveyors have exceeded their estimates by .£1,167 or 29 per cent. and intend tak- ing steps whilh will prevent a recurrence of the same.— Another matter considered at he last meet- ing was the street improvements at Stockton Heath, when the Surveyor's estimates were sub- mitted, and steps were taken to further the work. Gaskell, Rostock and Leonard-streets are the ones contemplated for improvement, and when the Council's intentions have been completed, all three streets should be a credit to the district of Stock- ton Heath.

Runcorn was quite alive on Tuesday nif;ht, con- sequent upon a rumour that a number of soldiers were returning home from South Africa, and large crowds of children assembled near the Railway Station, for the purpose of welcoming them home. The crowd began to congregate just about tea time, and as time wore on incrc,ased to such a number as to impede trsffic tl ana from the station. Notwith- standing all that Mr. Prescott, the stiVionmaeter and his offoials could do, the crowd would not dis- perse. Superintendent Pearson and a posse of police were requisitioned, but still the ' crowd ,hung on to their cherished hope; and it was not until a very late hour that the approaches to the Railway Station assumed their general appearance. Now that crowd is looking for the originator of the rumour.

One might presume that the town of Runcorn lays pretentions to bein7, a religious town from the fact of the many sacred edifices within its confines. It contains two parish churches,several magnificent Nonconformist places of worship and many missions. It is also the home of a branch of that excellent mission—the Mersey Mission to Seamen. Yet, not- withstanding, all these incentives to religion, there have existed, and there are existing to-day some quarters of the town which cm be "likened to the vile cancer that. hlasteth the good tree and causeth its fruit to be as hitter as gall "Let me at the outset Pay I appreciate the work our police have done to miti- gate the evil, against which I now raise my voice, ; but the parson and the broadcloth are" weighed in the balance and found wanting." In the centre of one of thes.- districts, wherein the sounds of vile- ness and blasphemy seldom or ever cease, there ' stands erected an infant school, to which the tender 1 ; child at its most impressionable age is dispatched daily by its hopeful parents. Whatever learning it may acquire is nullified by the vice and Contam- ination it is brought face to face with in its passage to and from school. And is this a state of things which should exist? Our 'parsons far out-number
omen

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN POLICE CASES.

On Thursday before Mr. O. L. Davies a sailor named Alfred Simms was fined 5s for being drunk in Waterloo-road on the previous night.. P.C. Wil- son had locked the prisoner up for safety.—Mary Iliz:tbeth Ann Wnite, a bad character, was sea- torwed:to 14 days' hard labour for disorderly conduct, Alfred Erickson and Olaf Larson,Norwegian sailors were each fined 5s and Costs 6.3 for aiding and abetting. TRIPS TO 3VERTON HILLS.

During this week ,verton Hills have been visited by numerous Runcorn folk, and the outings in all cas.s have been favoured with magnificent weather. On Monday, the Bethesda, Mill-brow and Kfiesmere-street Sunday Schools were the happy trippers; on Tuesday, St. iLdwards Catholic Schools, bad their annual outing; and on Wednesday after- noon about 500 of the Camden Sunday School scholars favoured the hills with a visit. Each school was accompanied by its several officers, and tea was supplied to each at the close of a very enjoyably spent afternoon.

div.p: RUNCORN SIAGISTRLTES AMUSED.

Davies and 8 Taylor, were confronted with a Norwegian sailor, Theobald Jensen, who had been locked up by P.C.Gregory for being druak the previous night.—Mr Johnson (Magistrates' Clerk) charged the prisoner, and it at once became evident that Jensen didn't comprehend. Several efforts were made to in iuce prisoner to speak b.nglish, at which the Magistrates were highly amused, but wihout avail.—Sergeant Pearson intimated the Police had only locked the man up for his own safety; and it being stated he had no money upon his person the Bench became more highly amused and laughin.ly dismissed the case. A BOY RUN OVER AT RUNCORN.

About 6.45 p.m. on Friday an accident occurred at Mill Brow. A boy, aged seven years, named Henry Lever, sou of a chemical labourer of the same name, living in Lightfoot-square, was run over by a cab driven by Mr. A. Booth, Bridge-street It appears that the boy was playing in the road when his mother called bim. The boy went towards her, and as she put out her hand to take hold of him he darted away from her and ran under the wheels of the cab which passed over his stomach. Dr. Robin- son was called in and found the boy crushed inter- nally, but the extent of his injuries could not then be ascertained. The boy is now reported to be pro- gressing favourably. SUDDEN DEATH Or A WIDNES PUBLICAN.

On Monday morning, Abnut 930, Mr. Samuel Morris, lan llord of the Sun Inn, Widnes,died some- what suddenly. The deceased had been ailing alternately for some time, and had received the at- tentions of Dr. Edwards. He was, however, able to go about, and attended to his business so late as Sunday afternoon. In the evening of that day he was taken ill. His medical adviser was immediately summoned, but, despite his assiduous services, Mr. Morris expired as stated,.from diphtheria. The de- ceased, who was 38 years of age, was a well•known figure in the borough. He was a great devotee of sport, and evinced a keen interest in the doings of the Widnes Football Club. His sudden demiss has caused a painful sensation, and much sympathy is expressed with the family. A. DAY IN VICTORIA PARK WIDNES _ _ ,

About 650 scholars and friends of the Oakland- street Wealeyan Sunday School, Widnes, through the kindness of the Corporation, celebrated the annual field day in the Victoria Park on Saturday last. A procession was formed in Oakland-street, and subsequently moved along Waterloo-road,Witt- road, and bowerhouse-lane, headed by the Widnes Subscription Band. Then followed the Rev H Barraclough and Messrs J II Harper and J Bennett (superintendent). The marshals included Messrs F. Johnson, H Tartan, J Harper, and J Odgers. Arriving at the Park the children engaged in recrea- tional exercises, and were afterwarus regaled with an txcellent meal. The outing proved most enjoy- able.

div.head: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS. --
div.p: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS. --

The annual teachers' picnic took place on Satur- day. The party, which numbered 25, travelled by the 12.13 train from Runcorn to Chester. On arriv- ing there a conveyance was in readiness to take them to Beaton Castle, a drive of twelve miles through some of the finest scenery in Cheshire. The early part of the afternoon was rather dull.but, eventually, the sun made his presence felt, and the country which was to be seen from the Caatle emin- ence was indeed picturesque. An excellent tea was provided at the Castle. On arriving back in Chester a ramble was made round the venerable city until 9.40. when the party embarked for the home jour- ney,Runcorn being reached in good time. The Hem H B Firth and W Scholes accompanied the trip,and Mr. John Littler made excellent vrangements.

div.head: RUNCORN MASONS IN WALES.
div.p: RUNCORN MASONS IN WALES.

The annual installation picnic of the Ellesmere Lodge, No. 758, Runcorn, was held at Llangollen last week. The weather, though at first somewhat unpromising, proved most propitious. There was a very gooi attendance of both sexes, most of the Masons having invited lady friends. Among the officers present were—Bros H 0 Linaker. W M, H Branch, I P M, E flicks, S W, T Foster, J W, W R Wass, P PO, D D of C; P M, treasurer ;T if Annett, PP, Or Tr, P J, secretary; W H Handlev. S John Litl ler. J D, T 11111, 10. The train left Run- corn at 8.1 a.m., reaching Chester at 8.38,and arriv- ing at its destination at 10 o'clock: After a light lunch at the Royal Hotel, the party proceeded by the river route to the Chain Bridge, At this time of the year the country round tho Horse-shoe Falls, —which is hard by—wears its loveliest appearance the rugged mountain scenery and the varying tints of the foliage combining to make a view at once striking and unique. Many took the opportunity to visit the quaint Llarttystlio Church, where a metal tablet records that Robert Browning, the poet, worshipped there for three weeks during the summer of 1891. After dinner at the Royal Hotel, the entire party were conveyed by 'buses through primitive roads deep jail the heart of the country, crossing the sources of the river Dee by winding round the valley of Llangollen. The return, shortly after tea, was commenced at 7,30, arriving at Run- corn at 10.10, the excursion having been a most enjoyable one. A HOUSEKERPRR'S INFIDELITY

Annie Johnson, aged 16-yWa-rs-,--a--Qive of Wol- verhampton, was on Wednesday charged before Messrs G L Davies and S Taylor, at Runcorn. with the theft of 4., the property of John Parr, an aged lock tender, 56, Irwell-lane.—lt appeared that Parr was asked by the prisoner some three or four week ago whether she should keen house for him. an arrangement he agreed to. The girl expressed herself a, satisfied with the shelter and " bit of meat" she would get and said she would require no pay. It was not, however, until Priday week that she put in an appearance. She stayed about eight days, and Parr bought her some clothing. In the house the girl behaved very well, but, Parr had occasion to complain of the late hours she kept. On Monday last the girl had been away, She went to Parr's by the locks, and he gave her some din- ner and told her to go home. By five o'clock he went home himself and the girl was not there. He looked first thing for his purse which he had left in an old tin, and upon finding it found that foar or five shillings had been taken from it. The matter was then put in Police-Sergeant Gregory's hands with the result that on Tuesday he arrested the prisoner at the jam works. She admitted the offence and said she had bought a pair of boots and stockings and had spent, the re.t in railvyny fare and food.—Prisoner elected to be summarily dealt with and plesded 7nilty.--M is; Hankinson appeared and stated she would take the prisoner in hand if allowed to do:so. and would do her best for her.— The Chairman said as it appeared this was the first offence against prisoner, they would allow Miss Hankinson to take her, she being bound over tor six months, to come up for judgment if called upon. _

div.head: BURNING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES
div.p: BURNING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES

An accident of a serious nature betel a furnace- man named Robert Fradsb am, residing at 10, Lacey • stre,A, Widnes, and who is employed at Aessrs Gas- kell Deacon's Works. Frodsham was charging his furnace sometime on Saturday morning when the flames belched forth, and in getting to a place of safety he collided with a pillar and was knocked down to the ground. His head was severely cut and his arms and body burnt. Foreman Hesketh dressed the unfortunate man's injuries and after- wards removed him to his home, wnere he was attended by Dr. Hutchinson. He is now progress- ing favourably.
THE CASTNERTKELLNER ALKALI COMPANY APPEAL

' The House of Lords gave judgment this week in the appeal of the Castner-Kellner Alkali Company V. the Commercial Development Corporation, arising out of the action for alleged infringement of a patent by the responient for the manufacture of caustic soda. The Lord Chancellor, in giving judgment,said: —ltappears to me that when Kellner,in his complete specification proposes to remove the mercury cathode, and to make the bells stationary:she is des- cribing a different invention from that described in the provisional specification, and an invention not merely different from that, but in its leading feature at variance with the invention described in the pro- visional specification I am, therefore, of opinion that the appeal must be dismissed with costs. My noble friends Lords Morris and Shand ask me to say that they concur in the motion proposed.

div.head: VIITTON BOARD SCHOOL -TRIP.
div.p: VIITTON BOARD SCHOOL -TRIP.

iThe fourteenth annual trip of the Dutton Board School took place last Friday, when 150 children, parents and friends journeyed to Southport Through the kindness of Mr. Jones, stationmaster at Preston Brook, three through carriages were at- tached to the 7.48 train, Southport being reached about 10.30. After a stroll on the promenade a most substantial dinner was partaken of at Hayes' Res- taurant, Chapel-street, and great praise is due to Mrs. Hayes for the admirable manner in which she catered. In the afternoon the party disparsed,some for donkey rides, others to see Pr)fessor Lloyd's great dive from ths Pier,whilst HOIXIti visited Church- town, the Winter Gardens. and other places of amusement and interest: At four o'clock a good tea was partaken of, after which the children were again dismissed until 7.10 p.m., when a start was made for home, Preston Brook being reached about 10 o'clock. Accompanying the party were Mr. and Mrs. Stokes (master and mistress),hy whom all the arrangements were made, Mr. John Kinsey (mem- ber of the School Board) and Mrs. Kinsey. Lurries and traps were kindly lent to convey the children to the station and back by Mr. Thomas Baxter, Dutton Hall; Jr William Fowles, Union Farm; and Mr John Kinsey, The Lightwood and Prospect Farms. The weather was all that could be desired, and an enjoyable day was spent. HONOUR TO WHOM HONOUR IS DUE.

Mr, W. Handley (chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Council), who presided at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, explained, to a crowded Court, that he had a pleasing duty to perform, which was to present a certificate to Mr. Joseph Savage, a young man who resided in Ivy-road, Runcorn, which the Royal Humane Society had forwarded in acknowledgment of his saving the life of a boy ( Richardaon) on the 28th of April last. Situated as Runcorn was with its numeroua canals and water- ways, they were often brought face to face with accidents of the kind, the sequel to which was then being recognised, and it was certainly a very noble thing when they found so many were ever ready to extend a helping hand to those in such circumstances. He believed that young Savage could not swim and had performed his gallant deed at the risk of his own life. Having read the certificate Mr Handley again exoressed the pleasure he felt at his task.—The action for which the certificate was granted was thus des- cribed in the "Runcorn Examiner" of May 4th : "A gallant action was performed last Saturday by a Runcorn youth named Joseph Savage, Ivy-road, which was no leas than plunging into the Bridge • water Cinal and rescuing a little child. It appears that young Savage was standing on the D(310 Bridge awaiting a friend,when he saw a little child fall into the canal immediately below the bridge. He ran down the steps and divesting himself of his coat and hat plunged into the water and secured the child. Being weighed down with his clothes and boots, Savage called out for help to a man on the Bridge but received no response. He after a des- perate struggle, however, succeeded in landing the , child on the bank and scrambled out. He went to the Navigation Inn, and was there given a change of clothing and some brandy. Considering that Savage had only recently recovered from a severe attack of bronchitis his action was most heroic. The child belonged to Mr. T Richardson, of the Bull Inn."

RUNCORN SHORTHAND WRITERS' ASSOCIATION. The annual general meeting of the members of this association was held at the Brunnerpuild flail on Monday evening, Mr T Clare, vice-chairman of committee, occupied the chair, and there were present—Messrs. W E Dailey, 1 0 Williams, J E Simkin, R H Bridges, E Gleave,R Gibbs, R Bennion, C Tomkins.—The Secretary rep3rted that the meet- ings of the association had maintained the interest of the majority of the members, and during the year the following hal gained speed certificates after examination by the National Federation of Shorthand Writers' Association ;—June 1899, Thomas Clare, 120 words per minute; December 1899, Thomas Clare 130 words per minute; and John Simkin, 60 words per minute; March 1900, John G Millington and Robert H Bridges, 60 words per minute. The examinations were based upon a five minutes' test. During the past 'session four lectures had b3en given. The library had been well utilized by the members, and mach benefit had been derived from the dis- cussion of out-lines with blackboard demonstration —The report of the hon. treasurer (Mr. R Bennion) showed that after meeting all expenses there was a balance in hand. Having regard to the slender income, tnis was considered satisfactory.—The re- ports and balance sheet were adopted, The officers for the ensuing year were elected as follows : President, Mr S Taylor; vice-presidents, Messrs. James Handley, F A Lak, J Wilson, J I Meredith, J F Moulton, R Posnett, and John Littler, sacra- tary,Mr Robert H Bridges; treasurer,Mr F Burrows; committee, Messrs, T Clare, W E Dudley. E °leave, J G Millington, A Senior, and I 0 Williams. The best wishes of the members were extehded to Mr E Simkin, a late member of the committee, who is shortly leaving Runcorn for Natal.

div.head: CHILD DROWNED AT RUNCORN. A Sad Case.
div.p: A CHILD DROWNED AT RUNCORN. A Sad Case.

On Saturday afternoon, Vlr. Rob 1.t.; D)bson. coroner, held an inquest at the Runcorn Police Station, touching the death of Albert Edward Grimes, aged one year and eleven menths, who was drowned in the Bridgewater Canal on the previous afternoon. Htnnah Grim,s, wife of George Grimes, boatman No. 20, Litton-street, Stoke.on-Trent, stated that her hus- band was captain of the boat "Union" belonging to the Andertou Company. The decoased was her son. Oa Friday the 27th July, the boat was being brought up the locks of the Bridgewater Canal at Runcorn, and when they reached the second lock witness missed the child. Tney had put the child in the hold near the front of the cabin, and not finding him there she looked all over the boat but without result. She then suspected that the child had climbed on to the hatches and fallen into the water. She gave an alarm and several people proceeded to'search for the body. It was recovered about 20 minutes or half an hoar later. Eff irts were made to res:ere respiration and witness sent for Dr. Ormsby but when he arrived he pronounced life extinct. Frederick Gibson, Sufi ilk-street,Rancorn, stated that he dragged the lock, and recovered the bo ly. Witness was on the bridge, and lvard the man Griiir?s give an alarm. He went to the look. The body was recovered in about 15 minutes after the alarm was rais!!d. Toe police and Dr. Ormsby ware Present when the body was recovered, but were unable to restore animation. The jury returned a verdict that the child was accidentally drowned.
A Horrible Discovery.

Abont 2 o'clock on Wednesday afternoon, a num- ber of men who were engaged in grappling in the river at ilowley Quay for the body of a child who is missing, made a horrible discovery, One of them named Thomas Pearson noticed the body of a young person floating in the water and it was at once recovered and taken to the mortuary. it was in a shockingly decomposed state, being minus the arms and head and the lower part of the legs. The clothing was in an advanced state of decom- position and the body is supposed to have been in the water for about a month. it was in such a state that it could not be ascertained whether it was that of a male or female.

Adams (medical officer of health). "THE PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY OF MANCHESTER."

Tee Local Gwernmeat Board wrote stating that, as the Rime orn Rural District Council were aware, they had for some time past had under consideration the question of establishing on a permanent basis, a port Sanitary Authority for the Port of Manchester. With that view the Board caused an order to be drafted, set- ting up a Port Sanitary Authority, and copies of the draft were sent for the observations of the Councils con- cerned. Cortain Councils however, took exception to the provisions in Article 12 of the draft and after con- ference with the officers of the Board the existing Port Sanitary Authority had been in negotiation with the oojecting Councils with the view of arranging terms that would meet the .objections. The Board have now received from the Port Sanitary Authority a resolution from which they gather that the authority have abandoned all hope of carrying out the arrange- ment which they had in view and on which article 12 of the draft order was based. A copy of this resolution was enclosed for the information of the Council, and it was requested that this new proposal might receive the Councii's consideration and that the board might be furnished with their observations thereon. Copy of re- solution:—At a meeting of the Manchester Port Sanitary Autherity,held Ia the Town Haliddanchester,on Monday, 18th day of June, 1900. Resolved: "That the Local Government Board be informed that this authority had tailed to come to any amicable arrangement with the Riparian Authorities within the port as to clause 12 of the new order, and had come to the conclusion that it was useless to make any further effort to do so,and that the Local Government Board be requested to obtain a permanent order, and form a Port sanitary Aethority out of all the commits abutting on the Pertsgivine them equitab'e representation and requiring them to contri- bute towards the expenses of sum authority." • Mr. George Leigh, clerk to the Bucklow Rural District Council, wrote as foilows,under date 29th July,—"Dear sir. the Local Government Board have communicated with my Council on the subject of a resolution of the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority on the subject of a proposed alteration of the constitution of the Port Authority. Doubtless a similar communication has been made t o you. As you are aware it arises out of a pro- posal of the Port Sanitary Authority to cast upon the whole of the Riparian Authorities the cost of dealing with certain infectious diseases other than cholera, yellow fever, lee. I have been instructed by my Council to inform the Local Government Board in reply to the resolution that there is no need whatever, in their opinion, for any alteration ef the existing state of things When the inquiry was held by the late Dr. Barry, some few years ago, it was then considered impracticable for the whole of the riparian authorities to be represented lon the Port Sanitary Authority, and it was then that the authorities now constituting the Port Authority were only too glad to accept the responsibility of working the I concern and of bearing all expenses in connection with it. It is since then, having got into work, and when the question of making permanent the Order comes up that the Port Authority endeavour to cast upon the other Riparian Authorities, which have no representation i•whatever and which perhaps like mine don't wants any, the expenses which they theressives unquestionably un- dertook in the first instance to bear. My Council trust , that your Authority will, after giving the matter their most careful consideration, be able to support the views ' herein expressed in their reply to the Local Government Board. Finally lam to ask you to refer to my letter to you of the 11th January last. Mr. J. M. Williams said be was one of the representa- tives of the Council who attended the conference, and could confirm what took place there. There was a great number of suggestions made, the first proposal being that they should contribute according to their frontaee to the canal. The Runcern Rural Council had about 15 miles of a frontage, and it was pointed out this pro- posal would mean a very heavy contribution for them. After several meetings at Liverpool, Manchester, and Hu acorn, an arrangement was come to under which any cases coming to their ports should be treated by tbe Liverpool authorities, who overhauled every ship thoroughly. Any case of infectious disease was to be isolated or taken to hospital, and the expense charged to the Authority to whose port the ship was bound. To this arrangement they agree' some time ago, and he (Mr. Williams) should entirely endorse what the Buck- low Rural Csuacil suggest,—that there was no need for any change. The Clerk said that these arrangements did not now exist. What did exist was th it the expenditure was agreed to be borne by till tiaras authorities, Salford, inches'er. ani Stratford. The Port Sanitary Authority agreed to the arrangement mentionsd by Mr. Williams, but tney could net get all the riparian autheritiee to fall in with it, and they now asked that clause 12 be , struck out and in its place a proviso should be made that all the riparian authorities be brought in,and given representation on the Beard, and required to bear their fair share of esteblishment charges as well as their own 008t8.
Mr. Williams proposed that a reply be sent to the Local Government Blard in the terms of the le!,ter ir the Bucklow Rural Council, that they were con cent with thP present arrangemeut.
The Clerk: that you are willin; that claus9, 12 should stand? kir. Williams : Yes.

J. Lawsols." Several Councillors : Bear, hear. THE SURVEYOR AND THH ESTIIIATES.

The Highways Committee reporteJ they had met prior to the Council meeting to consider the estimates of the surveyors. They begged to report that the actual ex peuditure, for the year endin2 25.-h of March, 1900, had exceeded the estimates by £1,167 or 29 per cent. £l5O of that was accoun ed for in the Frodsham District, by a special order given in respect of Clif:on•roads,Kingiley improvements ; and the remainder the survey ors ex- plained by the feet that the season had been a part cularly hard one tor roads, requiring more material than estimated for. It was the opinion of the corn rnittee that the esVmates should not be eseeeded with- out the surveyor getting a supplementary eetimate passed for such extra expenditure, and that it be a recommendation that a committee of five (consisting of Mefors Knowles, Wright, Baxter, Linaker, and Wood- ward) be appointed to consider the system of making estimates and the system of accounts kept by the sur- veyora._

T Baxter, in movin:: the a iop'ion of the report, said it was not a satisfactory state of affairs to have the estimates exceeded by so high a sum as 29 per cent. Of course, it was no, possible to strictly adhere to the esti- mates, when they had to contend with a long wet winter with plenty of frost. He thought, in the future, it would be better if the Surveyors would make special application for supplemen"Ary estimates, when such un- foreseen things occurred as would throw their eetimate so much out. If they could not see their way to do that, it would be better to take "the bull by the horns " and estimate for a much larger amou:A. The report was adopted unanimously. THE THELWALL NUISANCE.

The other had been taken annut 150 yards further down the stream just in Knutsford-road. This was described as not • good Effluent and not fit to be turned into a clear stream. Having dealt with the details of the an alysis Dr. Adams, in reply to the chairman, said in brief, the analysis, undoubtedly, blamed the tannery lot the greater part of the rouisacce.

A Naylor, Cuerden Half, Thefwall, Warriaqto,j. writing under date, July 30th, 1900, o Mr G F Astiton.Runcern, Dear sir,—ln roferenc, to your letter of the 18th I have had the prop.rty h-re examined and nothing wllich could be called a nufsanc:! exited. The only improvement which could be suggested ani which has now been made was to convey all drainage to one o,ss- p ;o1 and I shill be glad to show your Medical Officer and also Dr Vacher wh, t I have done if that' will make an appointment. Your letter speaks of setving tr,tices upon the owners of houses.' I assume this refers to the four owners of property other than myself emptying into the brook."—PS.—' All the sewage arrana, ments at and in connection with this place were approved and certified by your predecessors a few years ago."

• Inadvertedly, the following letter which gives Mr. Long's side of the issue has been overlooked, we give it now with apologies for our inadverzence " Grappenhall, Warrington, July 2nd, 1900. Tae Chair- man of the Runcorn District Council. Dear sir,—We have seen Dr. Adams' remarks at your last Board meet- ing, as reported in the "Warrington Guardian," and are at a loss to harmonize them with his openly expressed ooinion when he inspected the offending canard and its effluent some months since, when we showed him our arrangements and understood lihn to be quite satisfied that we were doing our best to render that effluent as innocuous as roossible,by taking out all the solid matter, and so administering the clear lime water,that it acts as a disinfectant as it passes down the brook. We believe that a committee of gentlemen of your board, after an exhaustive examination with your nuisance inspector, arrived at the same conc!uiion, We will not attempt to traverse the ignorant statements that have been made in some of the communications that have been addressed to you, but merely say that we shall welcome the promised Government inspection by a practical expert who under- ! scands these matters, and only ask that when he comes 'down he shall go into the whole question of sanitation of the lane spoken of as a veritably death-trap, and see where the offence really lies. We have a strong sus- picion he may find a different cause for the illness we have heard so much of,aud the deplorable deaths of two poor children. No poisonous matter and no sewage enters that brook from our premises. We leave it for an impartial inspection to say where, if anywhere, such danger exists, and remain, faithfully yours, William Long and Son."
