div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE. Half-yearly Meeting—Presentation toa
div.p: THE SONS OF TEMPERANCE. Half-yearly Meeting—Presentation toa
Runc-ornian.

The Cheshire Grand Division of the order of the Sons of Temperance held its half-yearly scssion at Northwich on Saturday. There was a good attendance ot officers and representatives from the various sub-divisions in the district, which compromises #uncorn, Northwich, Winsford, Crewe and Weston. Mr, William Dunbabin, G.W.P.i of Weston, presided. Business commenced two o'clock,the division being ()penal as per ritually Bro William Dunbabin,Grand Worthy Patriarch. After the initiation of a new representative the officers gave their reports.

The G.W.P. reviewed the past half year, and said that he believed the Order was doing a good work in tha district, and especially urged the members to pay attention to the training up of the young in temperance principles.

Tile G. Pa.tran of Cadets (i.e. juvenile sie!tion), Bro. John Brown, of Weston, gave a fall report of :be working of the cadet sectious. He thought that the members generally should pay more attention to tlao juveniles, and concluded by offering a prize to the cadet woo introduces the largest numner of rnemeers into any one of the sections during the next six mentns. Bro. 'Thomas J. Bolt, of Runcorn,Grand Scribe (secre- tary), gave the financial and numerical statement. Be was pleased to report an increase of 22 adult members, the tot,' number new being 561 adultsand 264 juveniles. The sickness experienced had been considerably abovo. the average this half-year, and had prevented the usual increase in funds. This seemed to be the experience of most fri.ndly societies in. the district, and it was satis- factory to know they were in a position to pay their members what was due to them when these exceptional times arrived. The Grand Scribe also placed the printed annual report of the National Division in the handre at the members. This showed that the order consieta of 46,443 adults and 19,720 juveniles, the total. funds b.ling £209,082. Tree increase in the adult membership during toe year was 3,668, the sickneste rate being7l days per member per annum, and the death rate 6.35 per thousand members per annum. The increase of juvenile members was 1,387, and their death. rate 3.60 per thousand members per annum. Reports of the working of the sub-divisions were. given by Bro. James Johnson, of Runcorn; Bra. T. W. Cooke, of Crewe ; and a repreeerstative from each sub- division.
Bro. Samuel Dodd, of Weston, and Br e Alfred Noden, of Rune3rn (auditors and bDoic-errnminers), gave their report which proved very iatereating, and was duly accepted by the Grand Division. _ _ _ _

A vote of sympathy was passed with Bro. Jamee Moores, grand chaplain, of Runcorn, who was unable to be present owing to a serious illness. The division adjourned for tea at five o'clock, after which the business en the digest was considered, which mainly dealt with the juvenile sections, and a committee was appointed to draw up a new cede of rules for them. During an interval in the proceedings, the Grand Worthy Patrisrch said he had a very pleasing duty to perform, and that was to present a framed emblem of the order and an ebony walking stick to their esiieemed treseurer, Bro. Thomas Heesom of Runcorn. The emblem bore the fellowing address, which he would read to the division :—" The Order of the Sons of Temper- ance. Cheshire Grand Division, No. 26. To Bro. Tnornaie &mom, Grand Treasurer,—We, the officers and mem- bers, ot too above grand division, have much pleasure in presenting you with this emblem, as a token of esteem, and as a mlnento of your thirty years Connection with the order, and also as a slight recognition of your valuable services during tnat time, both as a member, and an officer. We also desire to place on record the fact, that you were one of the zealous workers who founded our Grand Division, on December 20th. 1873, and th4.t you have tilled tbe offive of Grand Worthy Patriarch,Grand frustee,Gran4 Treasurer, and other important offices, with credit to yourself, and benefit to the order. Trusting that you may be long sparod Co C,ritintiq your useful career, wø are, yours on behalf of the Grand Division, Wieettee DCINIMBIN, Grind Worthy Patriarch; .fnoseas JOSEPEC HOLT, Grand Scribe. July 28;h, 1900." He then went: oil to say that he could bear tosjinDny to all that was said in the adtire.;S. The testimonial was the voluntary gift of the brethren, arid it had been heartily sub- scribd to by brother Heesom'e fellow-woikers. He had much pleasure in handing it to him.

[lto -Heesim, in reply, -said it vins; a pleasant surprise. Although the grand 83ribe and himself tukd been fre- quently together doing the business of the Order, be bad not said one word to him abut this matter. His C3ll nection with the Order had beAn a great benefit; w self and his work It id bei-on a Lib )ur of love. He thanked them for the kindly feeling shown to him by this tes:i • menial. Be should value it tsi the end of his life,and ta felt sure it criuld stimulate him to di more in the future than he had done in the past fur We good of the Order and the Tempersnce Cawe. Bro, Thomas Cooki, of Runcorn, said he had been a fellow worker with Bro Heesorn for a goJd number of years, and he knew that he had done a good work for the Order. His persistent and generJus disposition bad done much to help sn the cause, and had Also encour- aged ottaerd. - . .

-Bro Philip Leicester. of Nurthwich, cnd others gave similar testimony. A letter was read from Bro Daniel Bisbrown, of RuzA.. corn,regretting his inability tu take part in the presents-, tion. div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
troRE THEFTS FROM THE ARKET BOYS BIRCHED .

At the WarrimPton Police Court, on Monday, two boys named John William Forster and Frederick Forster, were charged with stealing from a lock-up stall in the Market Place at 9.50 on Sunday morning, seven packets of jelly, two trumpets, a ball, bell rattle, and five boxes of paints, the property of Mary Wilkiwon. They were furher charged with stealing from the stall on Friday, eight packers of j,lly value 81 —They pleaded guilty.— The Chief Constable stared that at 9.50 on Sunday morn- ing the priseners were reen in the Market-Place by P.C. Metcalf who was keening a sharp look out on the stalls on account of many complaints of damave and pilferinv. They were near Mrs Wilkinson's toy stall. The stall was on the box principle and the woodwork was nuilt round one of the pillars. There was a small appertwe caused by the wood not joining exactly so that a F mall hand could be inserted. The boys were busy taking out the articles when the constable saw them. When appre- hended they admitted the theft gni also stated that they had stolen eight packeti of jelly on Friday in the ewe manner.—The magistrates ordered each of the boys to receive six :strokes from the birch, Fiederick to be detained in the cells for 24 hours.

div.head: INGENIOUS THEFT BY A GIRL.
div.p: INGENIOUS THEFT BY A GIRL.

A girl named Annie Gleave, who is 15 Yeats of a", and resides at 5, Brick-street, was brought before the magistrates (Messrs. Birchen and Geddes), at the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, and charged with stealing fr-m a pen mbulator in Dial-street at noon on Tuftedae, a two shilling piece, the money of William Coolson.—The Chief Coniteb'e eald that the cid was charged with a somewhat in - enious and premeditated theft, which preyed to his mind at all events that she was by no means a novice in the Piemonte of petty crime. It appeared that a little girl named Martha Heath, daughter of Henry Heap, a labourer residing at heartirscroft, was sent by Mrs. Coulson, a neighbour, to Jackson's pawnshop in Church street. with two bundles to pledge. She was iestrueted to ask for 65 on each ef the bundles but the assistant would not advance Cs. upon the n but advanced 4s 61 on one of them and the eirl decided not to pledge the oeber. She brought the go-de to town in an old perambulator and on coming out of the shop put the bundle into the perambulator, and placed the money which she had received in a handkerchief which she placed under the bundle. She had s•arc(ly done so when the prisoner, who was quite a stranger, to her. came out of the pawnshop and fol- lowed her. She said" do not take that bundle home I can show you 3 nether pawnshop where you will very likely be able to get more on it. She then conducted the girl to Love's pawnshop in Dial-Areet and told her to go into the shop and she would look after the perambulator, The unsuspecting little girl agreed with this arrangement and went into the shop. She coald not obtain Cs on the bundle and on coming out of tri, shop was surprised to find that the prisoner had vsrishad. She immediately became suspicious and on looking at the handkerchief found it had been tampered with and the florin taken out. The girl then name to the Paiics Station and tearfully recounted her eventure. Inquiries were iratituted and in the after- noon Superintendent Monaghan and Detective Fester proceeded to the prisoner's residences They took the girl to the Polio? Station and she at first stoutly denied being concerned in the matter. When she was identified by several people c,he caved in and admitted that she had stolen the teener ani took the officers to the closet at the back of the heuse where the money was concealed on a Abe& Although that was the first time she had been ckarged with any offence this theft proved that she had at all events taken the first steps in a career of irepro- prietv and crime. She admitted that she had been ✓unning ac a loose end for some considerable time. The magistrates sentenced the prisoner to three days' im- prisonment and Mr. Tayler.the Police Court Miseionary, was requested te see if the girl could be admitted into a home.

That was no excuse for his conduct.—Fined 10s and costs. C ARRIAG 1: WITROUT A DCENB E.—For keeping a carriage without a license. Evan Edward Hughes, 10, Crosfield-street, was fined 100 and costs. The officer examined the contents of the bag and found two pieces of steel of the value of six- pence These pilferings were so very frequent and numerous that the sergeant felt bound to bring the prisoner to the Police Station where he was detained.—Sergeant Lawrenson was called and stated that prisoner had committed thefts before but had been let off with a caution —A fine of Ns with the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment was imposed. AN OLD OFFENDER —Michael Callaghan, who made his 46th appearance and was described as the worst character in Warrington was committed to gaol for 14 days for being drunk and disorderly in Bank-street at 11,30 the previous night. OUT OF His MlND.—William Oldham should have been charged with being drunk and disorderly but as the Chief Constar le was convinced that the man was out of his mind he was remanded to the Werkhouse for 14 days—Prisoner behaved in a very strange manuer in the dock. MoNDAY.--Before Mr. Monks (in the chair) and Mr. Birchall.

THE STONE-THROWING NUISANCE. —Charles Clayton (13). 15, Hoyle-street : Charles James (12), 17, Hoyle-street, and William Penn (12), 37, Catherine-street, were summoned for throwing stones near Folly-lane bridge, to the danger of passengers, on July 24th. They pleaded guilty.—P.C. Clough stated that on the evening of the date in question he was in plain clothes near Folly-lane bridge, when he saw the defendants throwing stones at the telegraph posts. It was a frequent occurrence in that district, in con- sequence of which he had been put on plain clothes duty.—The Chief Constable said he had received a representation in writing from the Gas Committee on account of so many gas lamps, having been damaged by stone-throwers, and he had placed constables on special duty. It was a perfect epidemic during the summer.—Defendants were tined 58 each.

BRFACJI OF THE PEACE.—Joseph Dickenson, labourer, Forster-street, and Thomas Salt, labourer, Winwick-street, were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Horsemarket-street on the 21st July.—Sergeint Bell proved the ease and defendants were fined 3s 6d each:
TCTESDAY.—B tfore Mr. T. Bin:shall (in the chair) and Dr. Ciornall.

A SBATILT ON A. WIER GoLBORNE-STREES —Stephen Turner. 27. Golborne-street was charged on a warrant with assaulting his wife Racine' Turner, on the 30th July:—He pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Steel on behalf of the complainant statod that the parties were married in 1882 and had four children, two of whom were living at home Three years ago the pri oner had the misfortune t • lose his right hand whilst following his employment and since then had not worked. In order to support herself, her husband and children the complainant took in lodgers and the prisoner seemed to have driven them away by his ab4minable conduct, making use of filthy language. On Sunday night the complainant went to bed with her two children. The man slept in the same rooom but.did not get undressed that night and sat on the bed threatening what ho would do for her. She went into the sitting room and lay on the sofa and on the following morning went into the bath room to wash herself. Prisoner came to the bath rocm door and commenced to make use of filthy language. Complainant told him to desist from his conduct and he burst the door open, came into the roo ci, struck her with his fist on the left side of the face, struck her in the mouth, loosening her teeth and causing them to bleed, seized her by the hair, forced her over the bath and said he would kill her. She screamed and Mrs. Farrell. the charwoman, came to her assistance. Prisoner told the woman to go away or he won d do the same to her. Eventually Mrs. Farrell took the complainnnt to her bed- room, where she fainted. Mrs. Turner had had no peace with the man. She vowed she could not live with him as she was afraid of her life. and she asked the magis ,rates to convict the prisoner of an aggravated assault, and grant a separation order She did not require any alimony, as she was willing to ke la herself and the childrm. Th- man had been examined by Dr. Braide, who would not oert fv I hat he was inaane.althongh there was no aoubt that he wa suffering from halluoinatiens.—Prisoner commenced to make allega- tions of improper conduct a ainst his wife, which were emphatically denied by the complainant —The Magistrates were satisfied that the prisoner had committed an assault, but not an aggravated one, so that they could not grant a separation order. They fined prisoner 1 s and costs (El 5s in all), with the option of 14 days' imprisonment. AN INCORRIGIBLE WOMAN.—Bridget Lally, a well-known character to the polico was charged with stealing from the shop door of John Gibbons. 99. Mersey-street. a skirt vain, 3s.—She pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable briefly related the circumstances of the case and add-d that the prisoner made her 61st appearance She had been before the Court no less than 11 times for theft.—The Bench sentenced Bridget to the maximum term of imprisonment—three months with hard labour.
WED:MD/T.—Before Mr. Birohall (in the chair) and _ Mr. Geddes.

A DESERTER. —James Mu hal was charged with being a deserter from the Royal Engineers stationed at Chatham.— P.C. Whittaker said he saw the prisoner in Horsem ,ket- street. and as he presented a military appearance he asked him how long he had been out of the Army, and the prisoner said he was a deserter and WAS about to surrender himself. He was a Royal Engineer from Ohattiam.—Prisoner was re- manded to await the arrival of an escort, and the constable was recommanded for the usual reward.

READY FOR AN INEBRIATEN iro—mit-.--Bridget Curley, An old and well-known offender.was charged with h tying been drunk and disorderly in Bank-street on Tuesday afternoon.—P.C. Wright proved the ease.—The Chief Constable ; This is a case for that much-needed institution, the Inebriates' Home. She is receivin4 a weekly allowance from the War Fund, and this is how she spends it.—She was sent to g Ise' for a month THURSDAY.—Before sfr. Chandley (in the chair) and Mr. J. 4epherd. WIFE ASSAULT.—Joseph William Allen was char Red on a warrant with assaulting his wtfe, Mary Allen, on the 11th June.—Complainant stated that at six o'clock on the evening of the date in question her husband came home and com- menced Musing her and making use of bad language. He at length struck her a blow in the la3e. Such conduct as this was a frequent occurrence.—Prisoner, who denied having struck his wife, was bound over to keep the peace in one surety of £5 and ordered to pay the costs, or in default three weeks imprisonment.

div.p: Warrington County Petty Sessions.

MrscELLANEntra CASES.--Samuel Hall, Burtonwood, wm bound over for three months for nommitting a breach of the peace by fighting on July 14th.—Joseph Lawton and Thomas Kelly, Burtonwood, were similarly dealt with for fighting on July 16th.—Williana Duxbury and Nat Derbyshire, Burton- wood, were fined ls and costs for gambling at Burtonwood on July 22nd.—Thomas Kirkham. Penketh, was fined 2s 6d for driving without a lighted lamp attached to his vehicle on the evening of July 16th. and John Lavin, Ashton, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Winwick on July 21st—Albert Bate, Warrington, was fined 5s for having been dr,ink and disorderly at Fearnhead on July 23rd, and for a similar offence at Newton on July 30th David Fraser was also fined 6s.—Thomas Smith. Galborne. was fined Is and costs for riding a bicycle on the footpath at Middleton on July 26th.

Taylor. HARRTET BAXTER AGAlN.—Harriet Baxter, a well-known character, and an inmate of Dutton Workhouse, p:eaded guilty to being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-st.. Runcorn on the previous Saturday night --Constables Wilding and Carrington proved the case.—The Chaiman said he had been present when the prisoner was brouvht up before the court on two ptevious occasions. She hid been given every oppor- tunity. but drink seemed to be her master altogether. They could not over-look her offence that time and would commit her for one month with hard labour as it was her fifty-third appearart^e.

-WIFE DESERTION.—Annie Done, wife of John Done, 87 Shaw-street, Runcorn complained to the Court that tier husband bad deserted her on the 141 th of July and made application for a separation order under the Summary Jurisdiction Act.—Mr H. N. Linaker, solicitor, appeared for the prosecution.—Complainant and her mother swore that she had been illtreated by her husband and that he bad tamed her out of the house on the date named.—Defendant denied any illtreatment but admitted he had locked both doors upon his wife. —Evidence was also given for the defence by Saab Jane Molyneaux. a neighbour,land another woman showing there were faults on both sides. —I he hairman said It was a pity that two young people who had only been married for two years should fall oat so • It was very evident they could not live together, and they would make Vie order for;separation. Defendant would have to contribute 6s a week towards his wife's maintenance.—Defendant said be would never pay. Mixon OFFE•CE9.—Thumas Norman, Cambridge-street. was fined 5s and 8s 64 costs for using obscene lenguage. —Mary Hughes. Collier-street, for a similar offence was fined 2s 6d and Si 6d costs.—Catherine Pali 1, a fish hawker's wife, of Princess-street, was also fined 10s for a similar offence.- John Warburton, of Weston Point. and John Dowd, Fryer-streel, Runcorn. were each tined 10s for drunkenness. —John Bazley. Stringer's-court, Mill Brow,was fined be using for profane language.—James McDougall, a reaster'hand on board a snhooner andrwho resides in Mill- etreet Runcorn, was fined 12e (the costs) for being drunk. INGENIOne BEGGING. —James Common, a tramp, pleaded guilty to begging in High-street, on the 28th of July.— Police Sergeant Gregory, who proved the case, swore the man had begged off a gentleman. His system was to ash fr a penny to get a stamp to write" home." He had been three times convicted for a similar offence. —The Chairman: Tke same man stopped me one day—Prisoner would be committed to prison for 21 days. KEEPING .1 DOG WITHOUT A LlCENSF.—Frederiek Inedd, of Weston Point. pleaded guilty to keeping a dog without a license.—P.C. Stephen Rowlands proved the case, aud said he called at the defendant's house on the 12th and was told he had no license for the dog. On the 23rd of the month he believed the defendant had taken a license out. —Fined 10a including coats.
Property under the Hammer.

At the Corn Exchange, Horsemarket-street, on Wednesday, Mr Thomas Tunstall offered for sale by auction, the workshops, buildings, land ard premises formerly known as the Cookhedge Glass Works, situate in Orford-street, and the two cot- tages and yards at the north-end thereof. There Was only a small attendance of buyers, and as the reserve price was not offered, the lot was with- drawn. Six lots of property in various parts of the town were then offered for sale, bat only one lot was disposed of, namely two dwelling-houses, Nos. 46 and 48, Lovely-lane, and the price paid was ..£550 Tee other lots were withdrawn. They included the leasehold dwelling-house, 48, Parker-street; thve leasehold dwelling-houses, 62, 64 and 66, Hoyle-at. thirteen dwelling-houses, 1 to 25 Vere-street, and eight cottages. 30 to 44 Wittkin-street. There was very little competition for any of the lots. Messrs. Woods and Sons, were the solicitors.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

ADOLTEEtATED MILK —At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday Ann Welsby was charged with having on the 30 May, at Stockton Heath. sold to one William James Hallard, to his prejudice,a certain article of food, ,to wit milk, which contained nine per cent, of added water, and which was not of the nature, substance and quality of the article demanded by him as such pur- -1 chaser. —William James Hallard,inapector,whose address was given as Chester Castle, proved the case. He stated that on the day in question he visited the defendant's shop and asked to be supplied with a pint of new milk. He told the young woman who served him with the milk that he had bought it to be analysed by the public analyst. He divided the milk into three parts—one part he took away for the analyst, one part he kept for himself, and one part he left with Mrs. Welsby. Dr. Carter Bell's analysis was as follows : " This milk contains nine per cent. of added water. This opinion iv based upon the fact that the sample only contained 71 per cent. of non-fatty solids, whereas average milk contains at least 85 per cent. of non-fatty solids. This milk has also been robbed of about 10 per cent, of fat. No C1130F.,,e had occurred in the constitution of the sample that would interfeJe with the analysis." The defendant did not appear in answer to the summons. Her daughter represented her and informed the Bench that her mother wag too infirm to attend the court. She added that the milk was sold to the consumer as it was supplied to her. She had ~put no water in it, There had been no adulteration. It would not be worth he while to do such a thing,—.& fine of 103 and costs was nfliated.

div.p: BOWLING.
Lancashire v. Yorkshire. Victory of the County Palatine.

Few inter-county competitions have displayed such ever-changing results as that between Lancashire and Yorkshire at Eleadingley, on Saturday. 6everal times the players of the home county reckoned upon a majority that scarcely arrived before it parted from them, and in the end they had to reconcile themselves to defeat. The Lancashire President and Vice-President opened the event favourably for their own team, but several of their henchmen fell short of success, and slender majoritirs were repeatedly converted into minorities. Not far from the close of the contest Lancashire needed more than a dozen points to bring them to the fore, and immediately prior to the playing of the final round required three to tie with their opponents. The final game proved a big success, and gave the win to Lancashire by seven shots. Score :

div.head: 144 Majority tar Maydoek. —......—. THE RUNCORN STABBING CASE.
div.p: 144 Majority tar Maydoek. —......—. THE RUNCORN STABBING CASE.
A Further Remand.

At Runcorn Polioe Court on Tuesday. before Mr. W Handley, Otto Schmitt, an old man, carpenter on board the Sailing Ship Celtic Monarch, was brought up on remand charged with maliciously wounding George Findlow by stabbing him with a knife. Mr. Burton appeared for the prisoner. The prosecutor deposed that he was a labourer and resided at 8 Leicester-street,Run- corn. On Sunday night, the 22nd July he left the Dar- well's Vaults Bentinckt-street, at ten o'clock in company with a man named William West. He left West in Brackley-street, and on reaching Bentinckt-street, the prisoner staggered up to him and asked the way to the docks. For fear tbe prisoner got into the water, he offered to take him to the docks. When they reached the waste land at the bottom of Trentham-street, the prisoner without speaking a word struck him a violent blow on the side of the head with his fist and knocked him down. The prisoner fell on the top of him and got a knife (produced) from his pocket and stabbed him seven times about the head. Witness shouted " murder" and" help "and in a few minutes West came to his assistance and pulled the prisoner away. Witness was weak and exhausted with loss of blood and he was taken to Dr. McDougall's surgery. He still felt the effects of the wounds and had not since been able to work. He was quite sober at the time.—By Mr. Burton: The prisoner was drunk and be did not think he was fit to go to the docks himself. Prisoner did not stumble in consequence of the uneven state of the ground. Prisoner was quiet for a time and he could not account for the change in his demeanour.—Dr. McDougall deposed that the prosecutor's bead and face were covered with blood when prosecutor was brought to his surgery. He had six stabs in various parts of the head, penetrating to the skull. There was a slight cut on the nose, and the right lobe of the ear was cut across. All the wounds were done by a clean cutting instrument, most probably the knife produced.—william West, mate of the steamer "Helen," residing at 38,Bentinckt-street, deposed to rescuing the prosecutor from the prisoner's clutches. The prisoner struck at him with a knife, cutting his j tcket through, and also his shirt and singlet. Witness then held his hands until Wakefield came to his assistance and took the knife. There was no hole where the prisoner was lying.—Josepla Wakefield, weigher, of 45, Bentinckt-street, corroborated, and said a crowd of people assembled and fasten, d the prisoner with ropes to prevent him doing further miechiet. —Samuel Battersby, storekeeper on the Ship Canal, confirmed West's state- ment.—P.C. Rigby deposed to receiving the prisoner into custody. On the following morning he charged him with the offence, and he replied" I can't say anything, as I don't know anything." The land where prisoner attacked the prosecutor was quite level.—The prisowir was remanded for a week on the application of Inspector Hicks.

1.0.G.T. Temperan—ce Mission Lodge. The usual weekly meeting of the above lodge was held on Wednesday in the Brick-street schoolroom. Bro J. [BY "QtruP 'N." I Have you, dear reader, ever felt that the air of your native town, the surroundings you are accustomed to, and the people you regularly tumble across in the average day's peregrinations, were all beginning to pall on you, and fret the edge of your usually smooth and easy temper ?—Yes, you have ! feel that way now in fact !—Ah ! I thought so ; it is the time of the year for distemper. I have had a slight attack myself of late, and not being anxious to consult the vet, with regard thereto, 1 prescribed for my own case. Pulse irregular (like habits), temperature 1000 degrees (in the shade), eyes tired of seeing same old things (office-desk in particular)—clearly a change required, however brief. It had to be brief, so last 11 mday was set apart for following the prescription. A friend being easily found showing the same symptoms in an even worse form, W 9 collaborated, and a short consideration decided in, on a change both brief and briny. Enterprising steamship companies had made such a thing easily possible, and the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company's trip to Llandudno, Bangor, Beautnaris, and Henai Bridge took our eye at once.

Monday morning found us on Liverpool landing stage searching for the s.s. St. Tudno, which was advertised to push-off at 10.45 and did so very promptly—in fact we only found Her Saintship at the last moment and scrambled aboard with a feeling that if the world was "wondrous kind" the people on the landing stage were not or they would have made a clear passage for us when they saw us coming at record-breaking speed. I rather like paddle-boats, they have such a motherly look about them; a kind of take-you- under-her-wing appearance, and the St. Tudno is an excellent example of the class. She squattered away in mid-stream like Some huge duck and was soon forging ahead down the Rock Channel with a goodly company aboard of "men and wimmen" and younger specimens of each species. "All was calm and bright" as the nursery rhyme eayet so poetically, hut it did not continue so by any means. there was a fine invigorating N. W. breeze bustling the ships off the port, and vary soon the "St. Tadao" was in the throes of perpetual and erratic motion. She didn't rell, mind you, nothing so undignified, but she increased her resemblance to the duck aforesaid by dipping her nose and elevat- ing her hind portion. We were in the latter part which we deemed safest, as a number of feAive battleships were manceuvring about the Irish Sea with a reckless disregard of neighbours. The "King Orry's " fate was not ours however; no untoward accident befel us either on the outward or home- ward journey. Rude Boreas and King Neptune had a friendly game of "pitch and toss" as there were no police about,and we on board ship occasionally took part, but nobody won anything that I- could see. Indeed there was more lost than won—which is true, if peculiar. One lady, who had lost her com- plexion, said she liked sailing "if it wasn't for that 'orrid cave.'" To be sure, the "cave" was rather pronounced and a lot of people seemed affected by the sadness ot the situation. Heads and hearts " bow'd down in woe" were common, while the number of earnest students of the deep was quite amazing. It was a "brew" day.l thought,and the sail verb enjoyable. People who cannot appreciate sail- ing when the ship does not keep an absolutely even keel ought to go to Belle Vue and practice on the artificial steam-propelled "ocean wave "there—and then tackle the briny. Presently little Orme's Head hove in view,and hope dawned again in eyes which were glazed with the fear (or hope) of death. Once more was terra firma close at hand, and when the St. Tudno "heaved to" at the pier-head,many swore a solemn vow that it should be the last" heave" for them and forthwith departed. Llandudno looked charming with its background of lofty, cloud capped peaks. but there was still the sail through the Straits to be enjoyed. Once round the rocky corner made by Great Orme, and the wind abated. The afflicted passengers recovered fast and by the time Pufflnlsland's barren shores were being skirted there was life and merriment on board once more. I need not dilate on the lovely voyage down the Menai Straits. You have all been, I doubt not, and noticed the beauties of Anglesey's richly-wooded slopes, the grandeur of the Walsh mountains, and the brightness of everything under a mid-day sun. Brief calls were made at Banger and Beaumaris, the pier-heads at each place being lined with a bevy of pretty girls who came either to see or be seen. Menai Bridge was reached at three o'clock, and there was just time for the hungry ones to get a "snack," walk up to the fine suspension bridge, drink in the glories of the view in either direction, and return to the boat. The return journey was much calmer, and the change to placid motion was enjoyed even by those who love a tossing—of whom fortunately, lam one. Liver- pool was reached at 8 o'clock, after a friendly tussle up-channel with the" Empress Queen" com- ing in from the Isle of Man, and the day's enjoy- ments quickly came to an end. We had had the , change, plenty of it, and our distemper was quite gone Warrington seemed the "good old town" once more, and we were truly at peace with all mankind when our " 'appy little 'ems" was reached.

There are, no doubt, a number of individuals in the town burdened similarly with the monotony of things and chronic van:a. Let me advise them to try the breezes on the briny. They will have plenty of opportunity this week end for the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company announce a special sea trip OR Monday, 6th August, by the St. Myles to Holyhead and back same day, leaving Liverpool at 9.1.5 a.m. for Llandudno, thence to Holyhead, due to arrive there 1 30 p.m., allowing about two hours on shore, and returning at 3.45 p.m., for Llandudno and Liverpool. The sail be- tween Llandudno and Holyhead is delightful, the coast scenery being unsurpassed. On leaving Llandudno the steamer crosses Red Wharf and Moelfra Bays, then passes close to Point Lynes and along the North Anglesey coast past Amlwch, Cemaes, inside the Skerries Islands to Holyhead Harbour. There are, of course, the usual sailings to Llandudno, and the watering places in the Straits.

A Peculiar Ejectment Case. At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. H. Neild (in the chair; and J. Tinsley, Mr. Jenkins applied for an ejectment order in the case of Miss Fryer, of Bell house Farm, Acton Orange,of which the tenant is Mr. William Beswick.—Mr. Jenkins stated that ttie circumstances of the case were somewhat peculiar. In the spring of last year Miss Fryer's goods were sold, and she had to leave her farm at Moore. She had a considerable quan- tity of stock of various descriptions, and she appealed to Mrs. B(38 wick, the wife of the tenant of Bell House Farm, to allow her to live in that house for a week or two until she could get another place. Out of pure kindness Mr.Beswick consented to allow Miss Fryer, her sister and brother to reside at Bell House Farm, and occupy a front sitting- room,and some bedrooms, and to store certain farm implements and odds and ends which had not been sold,and in consideration she agreed to pay a sum of 78 a week. It was understood at the time tat at the longest she would only be in the house several weeks, but she remained so long that Mr Beswick had become thoroughly tired; and he (Mr Jenkins) had done all he could to induce Miss Fryer to leave peacsably, but she still persisted in living in the house, and had become an intolerable nuisance.— Evidence having been called, Miss Fryer, an elderly and evidently an infirm lacly,said she wished to get out of the house as soon as possible, but her brother was in the Infirmary at Virarrington,and what could she do herself ?—Mr Jenkins explained that the brother had met with an accident.—The Bench, after a short consultation, made an order for eject- Went In3o days, and with this decision Miss Fryer appeared to be satisfied.

div.head: SPEECH DAY AT THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL,
div.p: SPEECH DAY AT THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL,
Canon Spooner and Education.

The annual "Speech Day" in connection with the Warrington Grammar Scnool,was celebrated last Thurs- day afternoon. There was a large gathering of students, mas:ers' and invited guests, the attendance including the Rey.E J Willcocks,(Headmaster),Rev Canon Spooner, Rector of Woolton(who di,tributed the priz2s), the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington (Alderman and Mrs Roberts), the Rector (Rev Canon Willis), Mrs Beamont, Dr. White, Misses E and S White, Mrs Willoocks, Miss D A Willeocks, Miss Smith, Mrs Wood, Mrs and Miss Pickmere, Mrs J Burgess, Mr and Mrs Carruthers, Rev R S Moxon, Mr J Young, Mr and Mrs F C Herzog, Mr WS Woods, Captain Waring, Mr and Mrs W Jones, Miss Calvert. The proceedings com- menced with the singing of the hymn " 0 Gentes Omnes "after which the Headmaster made his annual report upon the work of the shoot.

div.head: HEADMASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: HEADMASTER'S REPORT.

The Rev. E. J. Wreecomrs said :—lt is once again my privilege to welcome you on our aanual speech day. In reviewing the work of tbe past twelve months I can conscientiously say that the year has been particularly eventful in point of successes gained by our boys in pub- lic examieations—and further that a large amount of solid and quiet work has been done in the school: These results are due in the first instance to the unremitting and painstaking efforts of the teachine staff, and then to the hearty enthusiasm and industry of the boys them- selves. I am therefore glad of this opportunity of thank- ing you all—both masters and boys—for your loyal Ico-operation with me at all times. This year is also an eventful one from another point of view. The new Board of Education is an accomplWied fact. We shall now have practically a Minister of Education who will be responsible for all branches—for secondary, or such as is given in this school ; for primary, or such as it given in the elementary school, and for technical as in science and art scheols. This is certainly a step in the right direction, namely, towards the co-ordination of all our various educational systems—ter at present we are in a sadly chaotic condition in this respect. We are not, as a nation, enamoured of a central authority, but the want of it in education me-as the waste not only of a vast amount of energy. but also of a great deal of public money. Now that Warrington is to be raised to the dignity of a County Borough, our interests and just claims for consideration as the public school supplying secondary education to the town and neighbourhood can, I trust, be safely left in the hands of the representatives from the Town Council on our governing body. Among ether provisions the Board of E tucation Bill provides for the inspection of schools. Well, as far as we are concerned, we do not fear that—but on the contrary we welcome it. We are now inspected and examined under be Oxford Local Examination Board of Delegates, and we usually send in boys from the two highest forms to sit for the certificates of proficiency granted by the Boar"—Last year we obtained 16 certificates. Three boys commence residence at Cambridge in October next, and have WI passed the additional subjects of the previous examination, viz., G E Hesketh, entered at Pembroke College; C W Reynolds, at St. John's College; and J D Price, at Trinity Geneve Our other successes during the year include:—E Gandy, K W D Macrae, and H A F Silcock, who have passed the "Entrance in Arts" or matriculation examination of Victoria University, before beginning their course as medical students next term. E L Robinson and R A oolford have passel the preliminary examination of the Institute of Chartered Accounts. E S Kidd, late head boy of the school; Batmont scholar, and also scholar of Gonville and Caine College, Cambridge, has graduated B.A. in the first class of the classical tripos. GW N Joseph, of University College. Liverpool, has passed the intermediate examination for the degree of M.B. and Ch B. Victoria University, and has also won medals in physiology, in anatomy, in hieology, in therapeutics and in hygiene, and Wither has been awarded the senior Lyon Jones scholarship of £2l per annum for two years. G H Joseph. of University College, Liverpeol, his passed the t rst M.B. and Ch. B. examination,Victoria Univers- ity; R A Rap, the intermediate B.Sc. examination with- honours, London University ; C H Ferguson. of Univers ity College, Liverpool, the final examination for the degree of M.B. and Ch. B. Victoria University; R Pier point, the intermediate examination of the Incorporated Law Society ;R M Roberts, the intermediate examina- tion of the Royal Institute of Batish Architects; J R Evans, the final examination of the Incorporated Law Society; L Peirpoint, the preliminary examination of the Royal Institute of British Architects; R F Adamson, the Horsfall prize, Conway Training Snip ; F H Owen, the final exa flirtation of the Institute of Bankers. We have to congratulate: Mr E R Pickmere, M.A., on his appointment as Town Clerk of Liverpool; Mr R Dobson, on his appointment as her Majesty's Coroner for the Honour and Fes of Halton; Mr A S Kidd, M.A., on his appointment as lecturer in Classics and English at St Andrew's College, Grahamstown. Before calling on Canon Spooner, "ho has so kindly consented to swoon us to- day, to distribute the prizes and certificates, it may be interesting to you to hear the general remarka taken from the report of the Examiner, Rev. J. R Wilkinson, of Worcester College, Oxford, who conducted the examination of the school last week :—" I have had much pleasure in examinirg the papers sent up to me from Warrington Grammar School. The school appears to me fortunate in its masters; good teaching has pro- duced admirable results, and the merit is not only on the side of the teachers I consider the classical le andard a remarkably high one; the work done in this branch is, throughout the school, uniformly excellent, though not at the expense of the mathematical standard. I was also extremely pleased with the qoality of the French, especially that of Form V. Mo iern languages are, unfortunately, too often negleete l in our schools, whereas they should be looked upon as an indispensable mental training, without which no education Is complete. I obssrvcd that due attention is given to German In fact, the modern side of each form seems in no way to suffer from the high standard lattained in classical subjects. Due attention is paid to the education of the boys in the principles of science ; their drawing also seemed to be very good, and I was pleased to see, from a very good essay on India, that they are encouraged to take an intelligent interest in the affairs of the day. I noticed, in Form VI. a spirited attempt at Eeglish verse ; and I was pleased to see t at throughoet the school the boys had been thoroughly grounded in English subjects; while it is not superfluous to add, that the general neatness of the work, and the , i good quality of writing and spelling, especially amongst the lower forms, considerably increased my pleasure in examining the school. In conclusion, I mayremaik that the discipline and the general tone of Warrington Grammar School seems to me more than satisfactory." The Prizes.

div.head: Canon Spooner and Education.
div.p: Canon Spooner and Education.

After distributing the prizes,Canon SPOONER delivered an address. He said that he took a special interest in the whole question of education and he realized that it was their duty, responsibility, and privilege to contribute what they could t o anything that would help forward the interests of the Community genera,ly. He was sure their presence that day indicated not only that they took an interest in individual boys connected with the school but also that they took an interest in the great question of education. It had already been pointed out in the etcellent report of the Headmaster, that education included primary education, such as was given in our day schools and national scho9ls, secondary education. which was given in the one in which th y were particularly interested, and technical education. Be would venture to add to the list those schools of learning where still higher culture was aimei at,—h • meant the various universities. One felt in full sympathy with Mr. Willcocks when he said that the newly constituted Board of Education would aim at, as far as possible, establishing a proper and conseoutive connection between the three classes of education. They felt quite sure that the embodiment in this way, in one particular board, and in the hands of one particular minister, would tend not only to produce economy but he hoped, increasing bene- ficial results, which would be felt in the future educa- tion of the nation. The great object of education was Chree-fold. The first of all, was the development of' the faculties—the faculties of observation, memory, and reasoning. The second object was the fitting of a person for future life. Professor Ruskin had said that we would do well te bear in mind that every human action gained in honour, in grace, in all true magnificence by its regard for things that are to come. That was to say that human actions should not be con- cerned with the matters of immediate preeenee but should look forward to the future. He would remind especially the scholars connected with the school, as he would remind all present that the aim of education was to fit for future citizenship. But furthei than this and more important still he took it that the great aim of education was the development of character. He rejoiced very much to hear that the tone of that school was very high indeed and he congratu- lated the staff, the boys, the parents and the governors upon that most important fact because it showed that the highest aim as he conceived it, of education was the development of a high, noble, exalted character. Referring to the scope of education he said that man was a highly complex being. He had, as they knew, his body, his mind, his moral being and his spiritual being. He ventured to think within certain limits that any system of education, as a compute system must aim at the cultivation of all. He was a strong believer in a healthy body and he was very glad to see when he accompanied the Headmaster round the school premises that they had a very ample playground, and also la field where the football and cricket teams could carry on their games. Might he he permitted to say, if any governors were present, that he hoped in time a gymnasium would be added. Atehei the mental culture there could be no doubt bee-Luse they had met under the auspices of that school in order to celebrate the prize giving and chose priva were not exactly r.wards of virture but were evidences of a cer- tain amount of work that. had been done and in strong competition. Those who had won the prizes bad done so honestly and truly. The cultivation of the mind was receiving increasing attention,and he would remind them that if we were to bold our own with continental education, we must take rod can that we were hi the fore front of mental cultivation not only among the upper elopes, but among all the clesses of society. Pro eeeding te address a few remarks concerning the future of the school, the rev, gentleman said there was a radio., between the se-ondary and primary schools which was of great importance. In primary schools it was the obj'ct to give an elementary educa- tion as thoroughly and accurately as possible. He emphasised the importance of lacing a sound foundry Mi on n all that was primary. He sincerely hoped that those who had set a nntile example wanld find that the example Was followed by those connected with the school, and he hoped that the Headmaster would have the pleasure of announcing for many years to come, the names of scholars who had gone forth from the Grammar School and had obtained exhibitions and scholarship at the great Universities. In coneludine the speaker gave some sound advice to the boys and asked them to be honest, and truthful,and loyal to their masters.

An eVremely interesting prewramme was then gone through by the students, includino three plays in German, Greek, and Engliph, several Latin odes, and number of spirit^d choruses The plays were admiral)! presented, the b'y' acquitting themselves remarkably well. Sailors and Soldiers of the Queen.

Sir,—A great effort is being made by the Army Tlm- perance Association, to arouse public attention to the folly and cruelty of tempting our sailors and soldiers to take intoxicating drinks on their return from South Africa. Letters are being sent to Bishops, Clergy, and Ministers asking them to bring the matter before their people on or about the 29th of July. The Press are also asked kindly to co-operate in this matter,and so help on the work. 20,000 posters, of which enc,osed is a sample are being sent out and I shall be glad to supply one or snore to any friend who will undertake to place it where it can be seen.—Yours faithfully, _
HENRY TAYLOR.

(The poster alluded to Is a coloured one. and bearing a portrait of Lord Roberts. and figures representing the •• Absent-minded beggar" and the " Handy Man." A number of admirable maxims and proverbs form the reading matter.—BD. EXaMINER].

div.head: Shah. Exciting Scene in Paris.
div.p: Shah. Exciting Scene in Paris.
PARIS, THURSDAY.

It appears that something in the nature of a seri- ous attempt on the life of the Shah was made on Thursday morning. A man, who wore wide trousers, belt, and coat which characterise working carpenters in Paris, concealed himself between some vehicles standing near the entrance to the Palace, and as the Shah entered his carriage dashed forward and knocked over a policeman who was preparing to accompany the Persian Sovereign's equipage on a bicycle, jumped on the step ef.the carriage. He pointed a five chambered revolver at the Shah,but before he could fire,General Parent,the French officer in attendance struck aside the weapon and the man was immedi- ately arrested. On being taken to the police station he expressed regret he had not succeeded in his design. He is believed to be a Frenchman. His accent indicates that he is from the South of

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
4,000 Boers Surrender to Hunter. British Train Disaster.
Escape of Olivier and Five Guns. Tbe War Office has issued the following despatch from Lord RoberLe : ___
PBETOIIIA, WEDNESDAY.

Hunter reports that twelve hundred more Cif prisoners surrendered to him yesterday, and with them Commandants Rouse and P. J. Fonternel. In addition Commandants Deploy, Potgieter, and Joubert gave themaelvPs up to Bruce Hamilton, who had collected 1,200 rifles, 650 ponies, and one Arm-

strong gun- Lieutenant Anderson, a Danish officer in the Staats Artillery, also surrendered. Olivier, with five guns and a certain number of burghers, has broken away in the Harrismith direc- tion, but Hunter expects that his total number of prisoners will amou,t to 4,000. An unfortunate accident occurred yesterday near Frederickstad, on the Krugersdorp-Potchefstroom Railway. The enemy had taken up some of the rails, and a supply train escorted by a detachment of Shropshire Light Infantry went off the line. Thirteen men, Including the engine driver, were killed, and 39 injured. Smith-Dorrien had told off a special patrol to ride along the line to prevent any train passing over the very damaged parts. and a court of inquiry has assembled ;:o ascertain why this order was not carried out.

Local Policemen Rejoin the Colours. Oi Tuesday morning PC. Gibbs and P.C. Muskett. army reservists and tnEmbers of the Borough Police Force, left Warrington to rejoin their respective regi- ments prep tratory to going to the Front. The former went to Weuington Barracks. London, to rejoin the 3rd Grenadier Guards. and he latter to rejoin the Royal Garrison ArtiUery In Ireland.
A St. Helens Policeman in Fourteen
Engagements.

Cif Con3tab!o Wood, of St Been, on Saturday re- ceived a long letter from S •rgeant G. Shaw, of the 7th Dragoon Guards, vrh ) is a member of the St. Helens borough force. Writing from Camel's Drift, Pretoria,

on June 28th, Shaw says that he has been in fourteen general engagements, and about seven other smaller affairs, and has consequently had a fair share of the fighting, and pulled through without a scratch, in the best of health and spirits so far. Shaw's regiment has since the end of March ben under General French, and has had a hand in neirly all the dashing and numerous engagements that have made the name of General French so famous, and his cavalry such a terror to the Boers. Shaw received his baptism of fire on April 22, when pom-pom shells fell among the cavalry and killed some of the 8% EIUSSUS. His squadron was the first to cross the Vaal River on the Queen's birthday, and was afterwards present at Johannesburg and Pretoria, witnessing tre hoisting of the flag at the Transvaal capital at seven minutes pagt 4 pm. on June 6.

Captain Fletcher, Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment at Warrington, has left the service. Captain Fletcher has been over five years an officer of the local Volunteer Battalion. He

was appointed Second Lieutenant in March 1895, and promoted Captain in 189.1-1 e was popular with all ranks of the corps. Second Lieutenants Medley, Cary. Smith, Will- cocks, Gough, Roberts, and Williamson, have been promoted to the rank of Lieutenant in the Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment at Warrington. Messrs. Medley and Cary joined the corps in September 1898; Messrs. Smith, Willcocks and Gough were appointed in March 1899 ; _Messrs. Roberts and Williamson last February. Lieutenant Robertson, of the 2nd Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, with head- quarters at St. Helens, has left the service. ,He was appointed Second Lieutenant in March, 1896, and i was promoted Lieutenant in 1898. The Ist Cheshire Artillery Volunteer Corps under command of Lieutenant Lloyd,late R.A.,will go into camp at Aber to-day (Saturday). The following ' day the let Warwickshire Volunteer Artillery,under command of Lieutenant Colonel Owen, will com- mence training at Parkgate, Cheshire. Both corps will train for a fortnight. The Ist Cheshire Engineer Volunteers on Satur- day completed the special training at Chatham though the greater portion of the corps bad re- turned home previously being unable to stay until last Saturday. Second Lieutenant Fowler, 6th Battalion Liver- pool Regiment with headquarters at W arrinczton has joined the West African Frontier Force. He was appointed to the militia battalion indicated only last February. Second Lieutenant Ritchie, of the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, has been promoted to the rank of Lieutenant in the corps which he joined in February 1899. Second Lieutenant Burdett of the 2nd Battalion Liverpool Regiment, has been transferred to the West India Regiment. Years ago the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Re- giment with headquarters at Warrington consisted of 12 companies. It has now eight companies but it is understood when the corps returns from South Africa endeavours will be made to considerably augment the strength of the battalion.

div.head: SAD END OF A RUNCORN PUBLICAN'S WIFE.
div.p: SAD END OF A RUNCORN PUBLICAN'S WIFE.

On Thursday morning at Runcorn Police Court, Mr R Dobson, coroner, held an inquest on the body of Sarah Williamson aged 53 years, wife of T',omas Williamson landlord of the Waterman's Arms Q ue,ll- - who w.is found drowned in the Ship Canal on ru.esday morning. . . _ _

Thomas Williamson-, the husband, deposed that he last saw his wife alive at 8.30 on Tuesday morning. She had been strange in her mind for some months, but she had not been under restraint. Dr: Delaney prescribed for her a fortni,ebt ago. He had no reason to suspect she would take her life. Oa Monday she fell in tbe yard and this fall was the cause of her eye and nose beina discoloured. She muQt have had a " fainty bout.' When she went out on Tunsday morning she did not say where she was going.—William Walker, of 8, Hankey- street, labourer, said when he was coming to breakfast on Tuesday morning about nine o'clock he saw a pair of slippers on the ferry slip of the Ship Canal. Tnis caused him to look about and he saw a woman floating in the water. H. and the ferryman got the hoat out and brought the body to the slip. It was the body of Sarah Williamson. The ferryman, Richard Aspey, was in his hut when witness passed and Aspey said he had not seen anyone go down the slip Ann Roach said she saw deceased leave the house shortly after half past eight. Deceased asked her to tell Mr. Williams she wanted him at the corner. She told Mr Williams" Aunt Sarah "wanted him. They all called deceased Aunt Sarah. The deceased appeared strum. in her manner.—P.C. Wilding deposed that he was at the ferry a few moments after the body was recovered and he tried artificial respiration for two minutes when Dr. Robinson arrived and said she was dead.—The jury retnrned an open verdict of found drowned.

Bank Holiday Sailings. Several of the Liverpool steamship companies have made special arranzements for the august Bank holiday. There will bo a cheap excursion to Drogheda for the Boyne Valley by the steamers of the Drogheda Steam Packet Company, sailing from Liverpool, Collingwood Dock, to-day (Saturday) at 430 p.m. and on Sunday at 5 p.m. Passengers will be able to return on Monday at 5.30 p.m. The return fares are saloon eight shillings ; steerage four shillings.—The Isle of Man Steampacket Company 'olive made arrange- ments whereby all those who have the Saturday preceding the eank Holiday at their disposal can have the full advantage of the holiday from early Saturday morning until midnight on Monday, re- turning in time to resume business on the Tuesday morning. The company are putting their magnificent steamer Empress Queen on the midnight sailing from Liverpool. Those passengers who wish to have a full day only on the island can leave on Saturday at 4 p.m. Other boats available for return on Monday sail at 3.30, 4, and 6.30 p.m. The Liverpool and Douglas Steamers, Limited have also made special arrangements for the holidays,and particulars of the sailings to North Wales will be founl i -their column.

div.head: MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The Health Committee reported the rec,ipt of the following letter from the Local Govern:nent Board : Whitehall, S.W., 17th July, 1900. Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to state that, as the Urban District Council of Runcorn art aware, the Board have for some time past had under consideration the question of establishing, on a perman- ent basil, a- Port Sanitary Authority for the Port of Manchester. With that view the Board caused an order to be drafted, setting up a Port Sanitary Authority, and copies of the draft were sent for the observations of the Councils c -mcerned. Certain Councils, however, took exception to the provisions in Article 12 of the draft and after conference with the officers of the Board the ex- isting Port Sanitary Authority have been in negotiation with the objecting Councils, with the view of arranging terms that would meet the objections. The Board have now received from the Port Sanitary Authority a resolution from which they gather that the Authority have abandoned all hope of carrying Out the arrangement which they bad iu view, and on which Article 12 (at the draft Order was based. A copy of this resoluti ,n is enclosed for the information of ~he Cmacil, and I am to request that this new proposal may receive the Council's consideration, and that the Board may ba furnistpd with their obiervations theroon. —I am, sir, your obedient servant, JOHN LITHTBY, Assistant Secretary." At a na eting of the Manchester Part Sanitary Authority held in the Town Hall, Manchester. on Mon- day. the 18th day of June, 1900, it was resolved that the Local Government Board be informed that this Authority had failed to come to any amicable arrange. ment with the Riparian Authorities within the Port as to Clause 12 in the New Order, and had come to the con- clusion that it was useless to make any further effort to do so.and that the Local Government Board be requested to obtain a pPrmanent order and form a Port Sanitary Authority out of all the Councils abuttirey, on the Port, giving them quitable representation and requiring them to ontribute towards the expenses of such Authority.— A HOLMES, (Clerk). And recommended that a reply be sent to the effct that the Council very much regrets that the draft order had fallen through as it was perfectly satisfied with the provisions in Article 12, Subject to the proviso in Mr. Lake's letter of February 21st last, pointing out the necessity of fuller definition of the words "the Riparian Authority to whoss District the vessels shall be bound," and that the Board be informed that amngements had been made with the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority under Artic'e 12 and the Medical Officer of Health engaged to deal with cases under such Article. Also that the Council strongly urges that the draft Order referred to be made into a permanent Order.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JAMES HANDLEY, J.P., C.C.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JAMES HANDLEY, J.P., C.C.

It is with most profound regret that we announce the death of Mx. James Handley, J.P., C.C. of Holly Bank, Garston, and brother of Mr William Handley, Aldersyde, Runcorn (chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Council), which took place at his residence at two o'clock on Thursday afternoon. He was 58 years of age Mr. Handley'a decease was very sudden. Up to within the last few days he appeared to be in strong robust health, and took an active part in discussing public matters with many of his friends in the town of Runcorn, and no one suspected that he would be so soon taken away. It would appear that on Friday laic he was taken somewhat suddenly ill, wh,ch necessitated the calling in of his Garston Medical Attendant (Dr. Humphreys). The illness, however, did not yield in a satisfactory manner to the treat- ment of the medical adviser and on Tuesday ofter- noon Dr. Humphreys recommended a consultation with an eminent surgeon and also a pyiciaa of Liverpool. The result of the consultation was that the medical gentlemen believed that Mr. Handley was suffering from a form of disease that would render an operation imperative. On Wednesday forenoon the operation was performe 1, but at that , time it was feared with little hope of success and as it has proved the worst fears were realised and ,Mr Handley passed quietly away at about two o'clock on Thursday afternooa, much to the sorrow ' and regret of his many friends. Mr. Handley was a native of Runcorn. lie was one of four sons of the late Mr. Thomas Handley who in the first half of the last century was a boot manufacturer and merchant in tne town. In re- ligion he was a Congregationalist and possessed strong and sound views; whilst politically he was a staunch Liberal, always able and willing to give a reason for his opinion and Sir John Brunner pos-essed ,no truer or firmer supporter. When Mr. James had received the education considered requisite for a commercial career,he entered into partnership with the late Mr Gibson, as ironmonger and general furnisher, in Fountain-square, Runcorn. On the , retirement of Mr. Gibson the firm took the title of ' Messrs. Handley and Beck, and until the time of his death the deceased maintained an interest in that ba-iness. Mr. Handley, in tho course of his lite, acquired a wonderful knowledge of French,and could in every respect be termed a most accom- plished linguist. His appetite for travel was insati- able and to his friends it was well-known he would rush from one end of the country to the other on the slightest call of business. He visited Switzerland, France,and other continental countries and acquired a fund of knawledge that eminently fitted bun for the financier he ultimately came to be Indeed his ability as a financier was acknowledged and he guided many enterprises to a successful issue. He engaged extensively in quarrying at Weston Point and when the private owners there formed them- selves int) a company, some years ago Mr Handley was made one of the directors. He was also a director of the Runcorn Gas Company, Frod- sham Gas Company, Aldershot Gas Company, and was also an active shareholder in the great concern of Parr's Banking Company Limited, as well as a Trustee of the Runcorn Savings Bank. He was also iriterested in many cooscaercial enterprises ; his knowledge of trading and commerce causing his advice to be often requisitioned and highly valued. Retook a deep interest in public questions but the only local offiee (excepting his c innection with the Savings Bank), ss far as public bodies in Runcorn were concerned,was as a memb sr of the now defunct Burial Board, and which body by the way honoured him with its chairmanship. During the tenure of this office Mr. Handley was responsible for putting the finances upon a sounder basis. At a Cheshire County Council Election in 1899 Mr Handley contested Runcorn South again-t the late Mr Philip Speakman but was un• succes.ful. Subsequently, though, on the retire- ment of Mr Councillor Taylor from the representa- tion of Runcorn North,Mr Handley was nominated for the position and elected without opposition. He was a member of the Standing Joint Committee and of several other important committees of the County Council where his work was greatly valued About ten years ago he was made a Justice of he Peace for the County of Cheshire and about four years later he was placed upon the Commission of the Peace also for the larger and more important County Palatine of Lancaster. His knowledge of Magisterial Law was great and he sat regularly at the Petty Sessions at Runcorn and Gersten. For the laet 14 years or more he resided at Holly Bank,Garston, and upon the formation of District Csuncils in 1894 was elected a member of the first Urban District Council of Garstonsi position he fittingly discharged up to his demist!. By his death the inhabitants of both Runcorn and Garston lose a man of much pub- lic spirit, great knowledge, integrity and unblem- ished honour.

Good Templars District Juvenile Council. The querterly meeting of the South West baucs- shire District Council of Juvenile Templars was held on Saturday last in the Co-operative Hall, Earles- town, when Bro E Newman, D.S.J.T., presided over a very fair attendance of Superintendents and Re- presentatives from Temples in varioll4 parts of the district. The session opened at 3.30 and after the appointment of Credential and Press Committees covering the district,.the eiliperintendent Bro New- man read his report, in which he stated his inability to give atatistics,as the returns for t ie new quarter would not be due until August came in. ee wai glad to know, however, that the temples in the dts- trict continued to hold their weekly meetings even through the heat of the summer, although the attendances were rather lower than during the winter months. They must never forget that strong drink and gambling Were prebably doing as much (if nut more) mischief, in the summer than at other times of the year. . The regular we-kly meet- ing was a very valuable Institution and ought to be strictly adhered to. Several temples had already held very successful out door demonstrations and others were being. arranged. A great Conference hal also been held in Ltverpool,several weeks past, at which Bro J Matins, GCT, of Birmingham, Bro J W Hooking, GSJ T, of Gloucester, Bro J B Davies. DSJT of Mancnester, and other pro- minent numbers were present, the proceedings being very satisfactory. Several new temples were also in contemplation. One was to be opened in Warrington the next week. He also referred to the forthcoming National Com- petitive Examination for juvenile template, and urged that every temple should at once prepare for taking part in this very useful institution from which much good would result. Bro D Reid, D C treaeurer, reportel the financial position ta be satis- factory. Interesting reports were then received of the position and prospects of the Union Temples in the District. It was intimated that the Natiorial Council of Juvenile Temp'ars V?-19 to be held in Lon- don in October, at which this district was entitled to five representatives. Nominations were received and after several ballots the following were duly elected: Bro E Newman, DSJ P. Earle4town; is Mrs Duncan, PDSJ T, Liverpool; Bro G B Walker, P GA S. Liverpool; Bra D Reid,D C Trea, Liverpool; Bro H Woodward, D C Sec, Liverpool; Sister Mrs ; Walker and Bra A Francis were appointed altern- ates It was deciled to hold the next session in Liverpool in November. Thanks were tendered the Karle.stown friends for the excellent arrange- ments and the session closed at 5.40 for tea when a large number sat down At 8 p.m. an open air meeting was held in the Market Ground when Bro George Clarke. DE S. presided over a very largA audience, and was supported by Bro J Parr, S J T of Leigh, E Newman, DSJT and J Leatherbarrow of Earlestown.gernest addresses were given by the Chairmen and Bre Parr of Leigh. A duet was very creditably rendered by Sister E Woods and Mr J Webster and a melody was also sung by Br() George Clarke,Theproceelinge which had passed off very successfully were brought to a close at 9 p.m.

div.head: VIADUCT INSTITUTE, EARLES-
div.p: VIADUCT INSTITUTE, EARLES-
TOWN.
Annual General Meeting.

The Annual General M,-,eting of the members of the Viaduct Institute. Earlestown, was held in the large r,ading room on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. W. Emmett. J.P., presided, and there were present with him on the platform, Messrs C. W Emmett. D Harrison, W Davies, J Anderton, Joseph Emmett. T Ormaad (secretary), &c. The Secretary read the following report : Viaduct Institute, Etrlestown, July 31st 1900.

Mr. President and Gentlemen,—ln submitting the 31st annual rppert and statement of accounts we have much pleasure in congratulating the members on the successful working of another year. Following our usual custom we beg to offer the subjoined explanation of the income and expeaditure for the 12 months ended tne 30-h June last. Toe total receipts from all sourc are £403 us 41 or £3 3s 7d less than ler 1899. We would briefly advert to your remarks, Mr. President, at the last annual meeting with reference to a very limited number of memters having one of the three bowling greens sot apart for their exclusive use, for the nominal sum of £1 per annum. You then asked the committee to consider the advisability of continu- ing such an arrangement. When the usual applica- tion, for the use of a green was received from the club secretary, tho whole question was fully and impartially debated and it was finally resolvei that a charge of £4 per annum be made, which wae deemed fair and equitable, and one we believe m-ets with your unanimous approval. The total expenditure for the year is £403 17s 7d or £1 17s 14 less than for 1899. £l6 is 51 has been spent in replacing 114 of the 123 volumes which were found to be past repair or re-binding when the books in the library were verified twelve months ago and referred to in our last report. 358 volumes have been rebound at a cost of £25 44 31. This outlay has been met by absorbing the whole of the £l4 set aside last year for this purpose, the balance. £ll 4s 31, being paid out of this year's revenue. Shortly before the war began in Seuth Africa, your committee carefully considered the wisdom of having a service of war telegrams, or augmenting the number of daily and evening papers. Flavieg in mind their previous experience of war t,legrams, a costly method to us of ascertaining news which apoearedo on very many occasions, immediately afterwards in the nom and evening additions of the Manchester and Liverpool papers, and some times simultaneously with the issue of those papers, it was unanimously decided to increase the daily papers. This increased supply of daily papers has involved an additi mat expend.ture of £lO Bs. an outlay, We under- stand, highly appreciated by the readers.
