Towards which we received at the ()owed 15 4 10 given on the 6th November last 4 12 10

leaving.... ..... 10 12 0 which was voted in excess of that received, and which your Committee teel sure has your warmest approbation. Baud: In our report a year ago we referred to a graat of £5 to the bind, and in doing so said, " How very rarely the band eesits the Park to give members an opportunity of listening to a selection of music which could, we con- tend, be given saith so very little inconvenience to the individual members of the band, and which would, we know, be so fully appreciated and enjoyed by hundrees of peqele if a fix,el night,say once a fortniger, or once a month, from the begiuning of April to the end of S.ptember, vie.re arranged for Park music. We venture Co throw out this hint for the caretul consideration of the Band Committee, feeling sure that it will arrange suitable programmes in future." We deeply regret to rep nt that on one oecasiou only, and that very siaortly after the last annual meeting, has the band acceded to tee wish of the committee. If the suggestion offeree 12 montns ago and repeated again this year, were taken up in the same spirit as it is an .de, and carried out in a willing and efficient manner, your committee would gladly and in a suitable way recognise the goodness of th members of the Eerlestown Prize Baud io giving boat oleasure, which is in their power to give, to so manyeand which for s new unknown reason ha e hitherto been withheld. Can any member tell us why ? Concerts.—You will no doubt remember that a concert WAS given on the sth April last. when Mr. Lane, of Man- chester brought a choir of 50. In consequence of the limited capacity of the Institute, the committee decided to make a nominal charge of threepence each for admission. The majority of the members viewed this innovation with anything but satisfaction and expressed themselves as" surprised at the committee wishing to make money out of a concert which ought to be free." Such was not the case. However, their disapproval assumed such a practical loran that at 12 o'clock noon on the day of the concert 150 tickets only had been disposed of, and it ppeared from the returns sent in by the members of the commi' tee that very few more were likely to be sold. We, therefore, had no alternative, if the concert had to les a success in point of attendance, but to abandon the cnarge for admission, and this was done as you are all aware. The Institute will comfortably hold Oren 600 people which at threepence per head means £7 103. How a concert costing nearly £3O with a probable sale of tickets realising approxi- mately £7 10s can bb construed into " money- maki g "we are at a loss to understand. True we should be the gainers, by the value of the tickets sold, but the purchasers would also be amply repaid for their small outlay by avoiding the crushes, which have obtained in the past, and which will occur in the future unless you are willing to pay a am 11 charge made solely with a view of controlling the numb rto be admitted. If you are agreeable to such a course being adopted you may rest assured that no more tickets will be =old then we are justified in &verging of, alarays7bearing in mind the fact that only 600 can be made comfortable, whereas 2,400 (on our present mem- bership) can present themselves for admission to all free concerts. If any of you know of a better solution to an ever increasing difficulty we shall be pleased to profit by your experience and advion. Library :—With the state- ment of amunts is given a list of 141 books added to the Library during the year just ended, at a cost of £25 12s. 7d. This number brings the tetal of additienal books purchased in a little over five years, to 1,000 volumes, equal to about 25 per cent of I the number of books in, the Library when the catalogue was issued in November 1894. The necesalty for issuing a supplementary catalogue is Ireceiving the attention of your committee, and in all probability one will be prepared and issued within the next twelve months. Eight of the new • honks have a special, or indirect, reference to the War in South Africa Ifor they either deal with the causes which led to the , present trouble in the Transvaal,or show this progress of ! the Campaign since the war began. It is gratifying to I know that there is a constant demand for this clue of literature. Several other important 'works on South Africa, and China, will very rola be in the library and ready for circulation. During the year just ended, 8,052 volumes have been issued, the number of readers being 320, showing a slight increase as compared with the previous year.— Sectional Representation: In consequence of the steady increase in membership, and the very probable still ' creator number in the near future,the question of bettei and truer representation than at present obtains has tentatively been considered by your committee. The election of 12 representatives, as you are aware, is by a poll taken throughout the works. On the present basis cf election nothing can prevent the large shops forming a " combine ' and by so doing controlling the elections and returning whomsoever they will, against the wish and desire of the smaller shops who are entitled to be heard ie the administration of the affairs of the Insti- tute. This, fortunately, has never yet been the case. But the existing system is open to very serious objection because it offers the temptation to " pack " the Committee of Management witl. representatives whose true aim might not be to the best interests and welfare el the members. It has, therefore, been suggested that the Works should be divided into sections and one representative elec:ed for say every 150 employed. Thus br sectional repre- sentation every shop would be represented by the men returned, in each section, at the bead of the poll. The electors w mild then be constantly in touch with their own members on the Committee of Blanagement,to whom any recommendation cuuld be made for the better government and management of the Institute than can possibly be the case when men are in a sense irrespons- ible representatives. At the present time several shops and departments have no representative within reach, that is, in their own shop or department, e g., the wheel works, turning shop, smithy and foundries,timber yard, spring shop, moulding shop and the yard proper. The existing system is respeasible for such an anomaly as one representative in the smithies and forge employing 320 men, as cempared with two representatives in the bolt shop with about 30 men. The whole question will very shortly be more fully considered and a scheme formu- lated which will be submitted to you in detail before a General Meeting is convened, when the proposals can be fully debated and the scheme approved, amended or rejected. If approved, it would with your sanction, came into operation in July 1901.-1' ORMAND, Secretary and Treasurer.

The Chairman said he thought they would all agree with him that the report they had pit heard was an excellent one, and the 8 ne ~cretary had go into detail so very much that it left him next to nothing to say, and he (the secretary) had said it all for him. He might, however' remark on one or two of the suhjfc,s ; for instance he said that the Work's band bad failed to give the members that pleasure which they might have done during this very hot weather. He had asked for a reason' but what it was they as a committe., did not know, but if any member could give them one, in any shape or form, they would only be too glad to accept it and consider it. He therefore hoped the band would take the same hint this year as was given last

year, and appear on the ground, and give the mem- bers some music, which would not cnly be a delight to the members ol the lastitute, but to the out- side public. With reeard to the bowling green he made some remarks abOut one of the greens being monopolised by some of the members. The committee had taken the matter into consideration and it appeared they had increased the subscription from RI to £4. Of course that was a certain amount which went towards the increase of the income of the Institute, but be mi ;ht tell them that the other two greens bring in about £l7. so that they would see they were a long way short of coming up to the other two greens in their subscription. However, that had been agreed to by the committee, and be assumed the club would be satisfied with the arrange- ments that had been made. With regard to the concerts that room weul I oely hold about 600 members, and the reason why the committee thought it desirable to make a small charge was in order to prevent the crush. He was sure many people would rather give threepence not to be crushed than to go in free and be cruched almost to death, and their clothes torn off them. That was the sole reason why the committee thought it desirable to make that charge, but it seemed it was not agreeable te the members, and the concert would have been an entire failure, had not the committee resorted to the expediency of lettine the members go in free. If they were to go on the same lines they would have to have the crush. (Applause.) The question of reserving a certain number of seats at the concert was brought up, and the Chairman promised that it should receive the attention of the Committee. The following were re-elected on the Committee of Management, there being no opposition. W H Bailey, D Barcroft, J Barr, J Emmett, D Elarrisen and T Ormand. Messrs. Sephton and Liversage were re-elected audi- tors.
Messrs. Gee and Clare were rr-appointod scrutineers. On the suggestion of a member it was decided to in future have a Bible placed on one of the tables in the reading room.
On the motion of Mr. %V D3NifM4, seconded by Mr. D Harrison, a vote of thanks was heartily accorded the Chairman for presiding.
The Ch-tirman suitably acknowledged and the meeting terminated.

div.head: ........... NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. [By A CORRESPONDENT.] CRICKF.T.
div.p: ........... NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. [By A CORRESPONDENT.] CRICKF.T.

Earlestown journeyed to St. Helens on Saturday to play the Recreation team. and succeeded in pul- ling off in easy victory. With only six wickets down they had compilwl 132 runs, and out ol this total Miller had made 65 not out, and Al !emu 21. The cricket was of an excellent-, description, and the bowling of Alderson an Jenkinson was too good for the Rees whose total, all out, was 127. Ihe only one who made a stand [or the Rees was thack- lock who added 63 to tke total. There is a consider- able amount of rivalry between these teams, and the victory of Earlestown has been received with satisfaction.
The second teams nalt on the Earlestown ground but in this case the Recd. were successful, winning by 10 runs. Hatton for the home eleven made a capital stand for 29 runs.

Newton-le-Willows were far and away too strong for Winningz,on Park, winning in a ridiculously easy fashion. Winnington were only able to with- stand the bowling of Hindley and Ankh to the tune of 56 runs, whilst Newton put on 95 for the loss ot only four wickets. Turton, Mitchell and Carson were the principal scorers.
The Newton second team engaged Glazabury,and here again they had quite an easy task. Their score was 151, as against ,7qazsbury 37. For New- ton Hindley made 24, Harrison 27,and Sweetiove 26.

The Earlestown Primitives recovered their pres- tige somewhat on Saturday. Their opponents were t histon, and the match was played on the neutral ground, owing to a dispute the last time they met. The stake was four points,and the Primi- tives were easy winners scoring 60 to their oppon- ents 12. Morris ma le 14 and Mullins 12, and the addition of 4 points will be very welcome to the Primitives and considerably improve their position in the League.
The Bishop of Liverpool at Padgate.
Board Schools and Religious Education.

The Right Rev. the Lord Bhhoo ot Liverpool (Dr. Citavasse), preached in Christ Church, PaUgate, on Sunday morning, to a very large congregation from the words" Keep yourselves in Wye of God "—St Jude, part of the 21st veraa. T.. dis.uurse, wmun was iistenea co with great interest was on the sieljects of faith, work, and the love of God. The Bishop In conclusion said that morning their alms were asked for the day and Sun Jay schools connected with the churcu. He understood that the number of children connected with these schools had doubled in the last seven years. This place was rapidly increasing, and it would only be by a cer:ain amount of effort and self-denial that they would be able to keep their day school intact, He freely lick owledged the excellent scriptural icstruction which was given in the many Board schools in many parts of the kingdom. He had men privileged to see for himself what they were doing. He know, too, the high Christian character of much of the teaching in the Board Schools, and tbe ex- cellent tone amongst the children, but if a parish lost its day school the clergy and the congregation literally lcst their righs hand. Good as the teaching in the Board Schools might be, there was no certainty i,l it ;.and the time might come when a great change might take place iu popular opinion and a School Board be elected which would decide to have no religious instruction whatever in the schools, and then the present system of, for instance, the Liverpool Board School, would be swept away, but in the Churcb schools they had definiteness, they bad certainty. They had I children trained not only as,, thank God ! the Bo trd school children were trained,in scriptural truths,but they had them trained also on the definite and clear lines of the English Church. They had them taught in the day ! school what he loved the more and more he knew it and understood it—the old Church of England catechism; they had taught clearly and definitely the great truths which sometimes in the day of temptation and trial might keep therm from falling away into unbelief, and they bad certainty. As long as the Church of England remained what, by the grace of God, she was at the present they might be sure that the teachers in the day schools would be what they had teen—men and women not only apt to teach, but who desired the highest interests of their scholars, and who remembered they bad not merely a mind to educate, but a character to train and a soul to save. For this reason he asked them to-day to give as God had prospered them, to give to the funds of the day school and the Sunday school con- nected with that church such an amount as might free the managers from the shadow of anxiety.

div.head: MOTHER SENT TO PRISON FOR EXPOSING A CHILL).
div.p: A MOTHER SENT TO PRISON FOR EXPOSING A CHILL).
Distressing Scene at Runcorn

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, last Monday, before Messrs. W. Handley and S. Taylor. Annie Collins, said to be of Mill-street. Runcsro, was charged with expos- ing her little child in such a manner as to cause it unnece3sary suffering, at Runcorn, on the 29th inst., and also %I'll being drunk and disorderly on the same occasion.—Defendant pleaded gill:Cy to the latter charge, and net guilty to the exposure of her child.—Frons the evidence of Sergiant Brewster and Police Constables Edwards and Bratt, it appeared that the three were in company at about 12 30 on the Sunday morning, in Mill-street, and saw the defenlant and a man, seated upon some steps drinking whiskey out of a bottle. Deendant who was a single woman, bad the child, she now pro• duced in court, in her arms. The child was almost nude, and so also was the woman. The air was very chilly, and the child seemed to be affected by the cold. Con- stable Brain took the child off ter. The woman's dis- orderly behaviour consisted of first shouting and curs, in. and then repeating a portion cf the Church Litany. This she was doing to the man, and he was responding. Their explanation, for such conduct, wasi that the man had lost his wife, and she had come out of the house to sympathise with him. The woman was very drunk and violent and the baby was taken off her because the officers feared it mi2ht nonse to some harm It was her fifth child. Two of children were dead and both cases bad been reported to the Coroner. When prisoner was locked up she had created a great disturbance and kept the Superintendent and his family awake for hours, and another female prisoner, who happened to be in,had to take charge of the baby.—The Chairman observed they did not think justice would be done unless they sent the prisoner to gaol for a month for neglecting her child and so cruelly exposing it. She would also have an additional seven days for the drunkenness.
--0,- Narrow Escape of a Youth at Heatley. _

A serious accident happened at Heaney Railway Station on Wednesday afternoon when a youth, named Wilfred Green, of Heatley, had a miraculous escape from being killed. He was crossing the line with his bicycle, when an approaching passenger train struck him, and he was knocked down. His left hand was cut Allis forehead was badly bruised and his shoulder was also injured. Green now lies at the Altrincham Hospital.

div.head: Technical but hot a Moral Offence.
div.p: A Technical but hot a Moral Offence.

Several boatmen, fishermen, and labourers, in the employ of Mr. Richard Ab-1, carrier. Runcorn, were, on Monday, brought up before the Runcorn Bench, an ra charge of stealing on the 26th of July last about a ovrt- of iron, valued 30J., the property of the Unitei Mkall Company, Limited, and also with receiving the same knowing it to be stolen. Their names were Peter Johnson Regent-street; James Words, Wilson's-row ; James Fahey, Cross-street ; and Moses White, Lock-stre,,t. George Thomas Barker, chief cierk at the Runcorn Alkali Works,tescitiad 10 knowing the prisoners by sight. They had been engaged in removing s:ime rubbish from the works last Thursday aud Friday, f r M • Richard Abel. The rubbish had consisted of brick and old building material, but not old iron. 0-i Satur- day morning in consequence of what be heard he went to Mr. Howard's, marina store dealer Top Locks, and there saw a quantity of iron, which be identified as the property of his employers. The piece Produced was a sample of it. They had missed a con- siderable quantity of the iron, and valued the amount in the present instance at 30s.

'IJOhn Basnett, Gilb-e-rt=a-t-r.set, assistant in the emplof Of Mr. W Howard, marine store dealer, of Wate:loo-road testified to knowing Johnson, who e 404 A to i he shop oa Friday morning last, and stated he hid about ball a too of old iron and rubbish to dispose of, and wanted CO know if they would buy it. SubAiquently the iron had been brought there.

William'Howard,-son of the marine store dealer,ststed he managed his father's business. He had bou_zht tw° quantities of old iron from the pri-onPr W)0 for which be gave him 9s. and 4s. respectively. as 12d asked him where he had got the inn, and Woods repliev'' from Runcorn Soapery where some old furnace, were being shifted and the lion was given them for allowance. About 6.30 the same night, Johnson bad come to bins. and asked how much he had given Woods, for the iron.

Police-Sergeant S Gregory, and Police Countable Joisit McLeod, testified to arresting the prisoners, who had been charged collectively with the offence,that morning- Three of them pleaded guilty, but Fahey stated he WO only there an hour.

Prisoners elected to be summarily dealt with. eed Johnson, who acted as spokesman, said they pleaded guilty to taking the iron, but not to knowing it svae stolen. They had taken it, believing it belonged to Mr. Abe!, and that they were entitled to it for allowance. For had it bel,nged to Mr. Abel he felt sure he would have told them they could have it. The Magistrates' Clerk: Mr. ADPI did not say so - but'that is what you say be .would have said? Prisoner : Yes, sir Prisoner Johnson continuing, qaid they had made Be attempt to conceal the iron, and everybody could eee they were taking_it. Mr. Barker, recalled, said that Mr. Abel had net bought the furnaces, but was only employed co remove the rubbish at so much a ton. d Prisocers said they had understood that Mr. Abel ha bought the whole, which was the reason they acte" they did- Aaa

tile Chairman (Mfr. W. Handley) pointed out theta was no doubt that a technical offpnne of stealing WO committed ; still they (the Bench) did not balieLe priaoners had any intention of stealing, therefore ozei were inclined to give them the henfit of the d03",,-; They took that view.on the f:g it wa9 custata for the men to receive it as illowance, hut no thel been before the Court they wouid understand it 77,. stealing to take anything without express instruncionS," the effect from the actual owners. Prisoners were dismissed.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. ----- Cricket. In the precence of a good attendance of spectators Warrington played Bolton at Arpley on Saturday. The result of the match was a draw in favour of the home team, Bolton being all out for 172 whilst Warrington had knocked up 150 for the loss of five wickets. Bolton won the toss and electei to bat first, the pro fessinnals,Ellis and Poinron, being opposed by Dr Smith. and Thewlis. Runs came freely from the amateur, and at 27 Clarke took the ball at the town end. The new bowler's fir4t over yielded seven runs,whilst the first two balls of the following over Ellis hit to the leg bGundary. A capital catch by Briggs sent the senior professional back at 43, his contribution being 26. Owen came next and showing a tendency to hit, Bibby relieved Thewlis at 63. His first ball Owen drove for four, tut a fine break- back disturbed the middle peg. Slater came next, and a prolonged stand was made, several lucky strokes by the new corner causing the total to go up rapidly. Pointon continued his patient career, and though Pod- more was called up and the fielders spread out in cense- ' queliCei the rate of run-getting was maintained. Slater sent the ceeitiiiT up with a fine rive,and two runs later Dr. Smith relieved Podmore, whilst at 115 Thewlis took the bill from his captain. The score reached 131, when a brilliant catch by Dr. Smith. who fell after takir g the ball, brought about Pointon's d isminsal,t he latt r'slss being a faultless display. With the addition of five rune S aton got his leg in front of a straight one. H. Hargreaves assisted Slater to add 17 for the fifth wiek r, when a fine catch in the slips by Briggs sent back Hargreaves. --- Slater was sixth out at 153, Thewlis accepting a high return, the retiring batsmen having made 44 in capital style. The wits in his last three overs brought about the summary dismissal of the remaining batstnen,taking five wickets in three overs, Shepherd hitting him for three successive feurs, and was then caught in the slips. Mention should be made of the catch which dismissed Nicholson, whilst Hampson did not allow an extra dur- ing the afternoon. Warrineton commenced their task with J Callon and B Silcock, the bowlers being Ellis and Brearley. Runs at once came freely. and 20 were quiekly added, when Silcock foreed a rising hall into the hands of Slater in the slips. E A Connor filled the vacancy, and both bats- men treating Ellis unceremoniously, that bowler was " shunted ' for Pointon at 32. The separation was, however, effected by Brearley, that bowler getting Conno: caught at the wick et at 41, whilst at the same total Callon was run out, the ball rebounding off the wicket keeper's pads whilst the batsman was out of his ground. --- Dr. Smith and Thewlis were now associated, but at 54 the amateur as bowled, whilst with the addition of a single Brearley sent back J W Bibby,five wickets being down for 55 runs, and nearly an hour to play. G Clarke filled the v rcancy, and profiting by an escape at mid-on T he batsmen steadily gained the upper hand of the bowl- ing. Runs came with a freedom which aroused the greatest enthusiasm, and when in successive overs Clarke des- patched Slater twice to the rails, the spectators cheered to the echo. Thewlis emulated his partner's example, and in one over placed Elie three times to the boundary, all the hits being well-timed strokes. The century was sent up, and in the last quarter of an hour, both batsmen increased the rate of run getting, taking the aggregate to 150 when seven o'clock was reached Mewls made 51 in capital style, his hitting all round the wicket being a feature. Although favoured with a little luck, Clarke's innings was- none the less meritorious, and included in his 54 were nine bGundary strokes. The second eleven drew with Bolton on Saturday, Bolton being got out for a score of 168, whilst Warring- ton compiled 99for seven wickets. R Pierpoint and T Houghton opened the innings for Warrington, the bowlers being Cuncliffe and Seoffin. With 20 on the board R Pierpoint had the misfortune to play a rising hall on this wicket, and with only two runs added to the score T Houghtm. played on. Crompton and Duckworth 'were soon dismissed, and with five wickets were down for 46. Warrington were in a bad position. At 69 Connor was out lbw. With time drawing near, the home captain changed his bowling repeatedly, but E Pierpoint and flawtin were still together at the call of time. Special praise is due to flawtin, who played a great game for his side, having been at the wickets for an hour and a half. Cycling.
